caseno: Writ Petition No. 3773 of 1996 with WP No. 2746 of 1997 and WP No. 3834 of 1999.
lawyer:
Akhtar Imam with Abdur Razzaque, Md Shamim ul Alam, Hassan MS Azim, Md Tanvir Parvez, MA Aziz Khan and Md Manjur Kadir, Advocates------ For the Petitioner. 
Rafique-ul-Huq with Rokanuddin Mahmud, Md Azizul Haque, MK Rahman------ For the Respondents. 
Nikilesh Dutta, Deputy Attorney-General------ For the Government Respondents.
parties:
Mainul Hosein and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Anwar Hossain and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Joynul Abedin J: Since common questions of law and fact are involved in all these three writ petitions, Rules in all these writ petitions are heard and disposed of by this single judgment.

2. In writ petition No. 3773 of 1996, Rule Nisi is issued calling upon the respondent No. 1 Mr Anwar Hossain, to show cause as to why he should not be prohibited from holding the post and position of the Executive Director-II, Editor, Printer and Publisher of the Daily lttefaq as he is debarred from acting as such under Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

3. In Writ Petition No. 2146 of 1997, Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents, the District Magistrate and the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka and Mr Anwar Hossain, to show cause as to why the impugned orders contained in Annexures-E and G and the publication of name of respondent No.3, Mr Anwar Hossain, as printer and publisher on behalf of the petitioner No.2, Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd, should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

4. In Writ Petition No. 3834 of 1999, Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondent, Mr Anwar Hossain, to show cause as to why his acts of issuing the impugned orders contained in Annexures-A, A1 and A-2 directly taking part in the management and running of the business of the petitioner No.2, Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd, should not be declared to have been made illegally and without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

5. The broad facts leading to the issuance of the aforesaid Rules are substantially the same which are shortly stated as under:

Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd, Petitioner No.2, in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 and Writ Petition No. 3834 of 1999, is a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act on 31-1-1970 which, among others, took over the management and publications of the national daily, Daily lttefaq, together with other business as indicated in its Memorandum of Association. The management and publications of the said prestigious daily were made by the heirs of late Mr Tofazzal Hossain (Manik Mia) including the petitioner Mr Mainul Hosein and respondent Mr Anwar Hossain as sons of late Mr Manik Mia with a view to collectively owning and continuing with the publication of the said daily. From the inception of the said Company petitioner Mr Mainul Hosein was made the Executive Director-I and respondent Mr Anwar Hossain was made the Executive Director-Il and they constituted the Executive Committee as a mini Board of Directors of the said Company as provided in Article 52 of the Articles of Association of the Company. The concept of the Executive Committee in the Articles of Association of the said Company was devised for the purpose of conferring joint responsibility on the two executive directors in the matters of running the business of the Company including the management and the publications of the Daily Ittefaq so that the Company can function smoothly without referring almost every matter to the Board of Directors for decision.

6. From the inception of the publication of the said premier daily petitioner Mr Mainul Hosein was made the Editor of the said newspaper and late Mr Motahar Hossain Siddiki, a family friend of late Mr Manik Mia, was made to act as the printer and publisher for the said daily. Subsequently, the Company appointed the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain, Editor of the Daily Ittefaq by a resolution dated 10-3-1972 in .place of the petitioner. Mr Mainul Hosein and Mr Mainul Hosein became the Chairman of the Board of Editors as he wanted to spend more of his time in the profession of Law.

7. When the aforesaid daily was being published and run under the arrangement as above, respondent Mr Anwar Hossain suddenly joined the cabinet of General HM Ershad's Government on 26-3-85. Mr Motahar Hossain Siddiki, thereupon, as the printer and publisher of the Daily Ittefaq, informed the District Magistrate, Dhaka that respondent Mr Anwar Hossain was no longer functioning as the Editor and the Senior Assistant Editor of the paper Mr Akhtarul Alam would act as the Editor until further decision: Mr Anwar Hossain, in spite of his becoming a Minister, wanted to continue as the Editor but did not get any support from the Directors and the Shareholders of the Company. In this situation, the Directors and the Shareholders of the Company passed a resolution dated 29-3-85 making Mr Anwar Hossain the Publisher and Mr Mainul Hosein the Printer of the Daily Ittefaq after removing the family friend Mr Motahar Hossain Siddiki. On the following day on 30-3-85 another resolution was passed by the Company appointing Mr Anwar Hossain as the printer and publisher on behalf of the Company in place of Mr Motahar Hossain Siddiki. Mr Motahar Hossain Siddiki resigned as the printer and publisher of the Company by giving a declaration in Form C on 21-4-85 and on the same date i.e. 21-4- 85 Mr Anwar Hossain made a declaration in Form B under section 7 of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 as printer and publisher of the Daily Ittefaq for the Company.

8. Although Mr Anwar Hossain was made the Printer, Publisher and the Editor for the Daily Ittefaq, the joint responsibility for the duties of the editor was given to both Mr Mainul Hosein and Mr Anwar Hossain by a resolution dated 27-10-1986 in this behalf. Mr Anwar Hossain continued as the Minister under the Martial Law Government of HM Ershad upto 6-12-90 and Mr Akhtarul Alam continued as the Editor-in-Charge for the Daily Ittefaq. Eventually, Mr Akhtarul Alam was appointed as Ambassador for Bangladesh to Bahrain and the publication of his name as Editor-in-Charge was dis-continued with effect from 15-4-92. Meanwhile, due to administrative deadlock the Daily Ittefaq was not published from 28-12-93 to 3- 1-94 and with the resumption of the publication of the Daily Ittefaq Mr Anwar Hossain by show of power and using muscle power of his political patty got his name forcibly published as Editor without caring to take the matter to the Board of Directors for a decision. Although the post of the Editor fell vacant on his becoming Minister it was not possible for the Company to appoint a new editor because of the non-cooperation of Mr Anwar Hossain in this regard. Accordingly, the name of Mr Rahat Khan had been published as Editor-in-Charge.

9. At this time the petitioner Mr Mainul Hosein came to learn from the letter dated 4-2-97 addressed by the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka to respondent Mr Anwar Hossain, that the Additional District Magistrate had accepted Mr Anwar Hossain as the publisher without any reference to the Company although the Company itself was and still is the publisher and Mr Anwar Hossain was performing as the publisher for the Company. The Additional District Magistrate by the said letter informed that his office had no objection if Mr Rahat Khan discharged the functions as editor- in charge during the period of absence of the Editor, Mr Anwar Hossain. This letter dated 4-2-97 is impugned as Annexure-E to the writ petition No. 2746 of 1997. The petitioner Mr Mainul Hosein, thereupon, addressed a letter dated 12-3-97 to the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka clarifying that Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd was, in fact, the printer and publisher and Mr Anwar Hossain had been acting as the printer and publisher of the Daily Ittefaq for the Company. Mr Mainul Hosein also informed by the said letter that Mr Anwar Hossain ceased to be the Editor of the Daily Ittefaq when he entered the office of the Minister by operation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution and Mr Rahat Khan became the Editor as there was no such position as editor-in-charge or acting editor under the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973" consequently Mr Anwar Hossain should not therefore, be considered as the Editor of the said daily, Subsequently, the Additional District Magistrate addressed a letter dated 3-4-97 in reply to his letter dated 12-3-97 informing Mr Mainul Hosein that Mr Anwar Hossain was the printer and publisher of the Daily Ittefaq and he alone had the power and authority to decide as to who would discharge the functions as the Editor during his absence as Editor. This letter dated 3-4-97 is impugned as Annexure-G to the Writ Petition No. 2786 of 1997.

10. While Mr Anwar Hossain was continuing as a Minister under the consensus government of the  Awami League he ceased to be the printer, publisher and Editor of the Daily Ittefaq. In this situation, Mr Anwar Hossain passed certain orders dated 23-1-99, 17-8-99 and 25-9-99 terminating services of some employees and appointing someone in the employment of the said Company, which amounted to taking part in the management or conduct of the said Company although he was debarred from doing so as contemplated under Article 147(3) of the Constitution. These actions of Mr Anwar Hossain terminating services of two employees and appointing a person in the employment of the said Company, as evident in Annexures-A, A-1 and A-2, have been impugned in Writ petition No. 3834 of 1999.

11. Respondent Mr Anwar Hossain has contested the Rules in all the aforesaid writ petitions by filing affidavit-in-opposition. Respondent Anwar Hossain having admitted the broad statements contained in all the writ petitions has contended that he became the Printer. Publisher and Editor of the Daily Ittefaq as per the decision of the Company as reflected in its various resolutions. But he never ceased to be the printer, publisher and editor by operation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution as alleged by the petitioner. It is contended in the affidavit-in-opposition that the aforesaid claim of the petitioner was misconceived being based on misconstruction of Article 147(3) of the Constitution. The position of Mr Anwar Hossain as the Printer, Publisher and Editor of the Daily Ittefaq not having been affected by his becoming the. Minister there was no necessity of appointing anyone as the printer, publisher and also as the Editor of the Daily Ittefaq. Hence; initially Mr Akhtarul Alam was appointed as editor-in-charge in , the absence of Mr Anwar Hossain and he (Akhtarul Alam) continued as such without any objection from any quarters during the period Mr Anwar Hossain became a Minister in the Cabinet of Mr Ershad's Government. Similarly, Mr Rahat Khan was appointed by him as the acting editor during his absence when he became the Minister in the consensus government of the Awami League. Since the post of printer, publisher and editor of the Daily Ittefaq never fell vacant while Mr Anwar Hossain became Minister twice there was no necessity of making any fresh declaration as regards the printer, publisher and editor under section 7 and authentication of the declaration under section 12 of the Printing Presses and Publications Act, 1973. Hence, the communications made by the Additional District. Magistrate, Dhaka in this regard and impugned in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 were in accordance with law. It is also stated in the affidavit-in-opposition filed by Mr Anwar Hossain in Writ Petition No. 3834 of 1999 that since those impugned orders regarding dismissal and appointment of some persons in the Company were subsequently withdrawn Rule in the said writ petition became infructuous.

12. Respondents 1 and, 2, the District Magistrate and the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka, have also appeared and contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 echoing the same view as taken by Mr Anwar Hossain stating that Mr Anwar Hossain never ceased to be the Printer, Publisher and Editor by operation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution after he held the office of the Minister. Hence, Mr Anwar Hossain acted in accordance with law in appointing Mr Rahat Khan as an acting editor of the Daily Ittefaq during his absence. Accordingly, they had no objection if Mr Rahat Khan acted as the acting editor for him. The petitioners and the respondents have also reiterated their respective case by filing affidavit-in-reply and supplementary affidavit-in-opposition.

13. Mr Akhtar Imam and Mr Abdur Razzaque, the learned Counsels appearing for the petitioners, have taken us through the writ petitions, affidavit and supplementary affidavit-in-opposition and affidavit and supplementary affidavit-in-reply including the annexures. The learned Counsels have also placed Article 147(3) of the Constitution and various sections of the Printing Presses and Publications Act, 1973 and submitted that by operation of Article 147(3) Mr Anwar Hossain has ceased to be the Executive Director-Il in Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd and also the Printer, Publisher and the Editor of the Daily Ittefaq the moment he held the office of the Minister. While elaborating this submission, the learned Counsels argued that since Article 147(3) is couched in negative terms its effect is mandatory. Hence the bar created by clause (3) of Article 147 against holding the office, post or position of the printer, publisher and editor is total and absolute meaning that the bar is permanent and is not temporary such as till he holds the office of the Minister.

14. In support of this contention, Mr Akhtar Imam has placed reliance in the case of Osman Gani Mondal vs Mainuddin Ahmed and others reported in 27 DLR (AD) 61. With regard to the 'proviso' to Article 147(3), both the learned Counsels contend that it (proviso) merely declares that the offices specified in clause (4) of Article 147(3) including the office of the Minister are not the offices of profit and not that it excludes the office, post or position held by the President, Prime Minister, Minister, Speaker, etc. in any company, body or association immediately before he became the President, Prime Minister, Speaker, etc from being the office, post or position of profit or emolument. Constitutional Law of Bangladesh, 2nd Edition, paragraph 6.59B by Mahmudul Islam is also referred to. in this connection. The learned Counsels also submit that since Mr Anwar Hossain has ceased to be the Printer, Publisher and Editor on his assumption of office as Minister he was not competent under the Printing Presses and Publications Act, 1973 to appoint Mr Rahat Khan as the acting editor and inform or notify the same to the District Magistrate or Additional District Magistrate. Mr Anwar Hossain, according to the learned Counsels, was required to make a fresh declaration for authentication with Mr Rahat Khan, as Editor under sections 7 and 12 of the said Act, 1973. Additional District Magistrate, it is argued, having accepted the mere intimation of Mr Anwar Hossain that Mr Rahat Khan was appointed by him as an acting editor during his absence without requiring Mr Anwar Hossain to make a fresh declaration for authentication that Mr Rahat Khan was appointed as the Editor acted illegally. Hence the impugned Annexures E and G in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 are liable to be struck down as unlawful.

15. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent Anwar Hossain in all the writ petitions, opposes the Rules on the following grounds:

(a) Rules in Writ Petition Nos. 3773 of 1996 and 3834 of 1999 are not maintainable under Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution inasmuch as the impugned acts or omissions were not committed by Mr Anwar Hossain in the affairs of the Republic or a local authority as required under Article 102(2) but in relation to or in the affairs of Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd, a private limited company incorporated under the Companies Act.

(b) Since admittedly, some civil suits are pending involving adjudication of the same points as in these 3(three) writ petitions, Rules are liable to be discharged as not maintainable as the petitioners cannot invoke both the jurisdictions for the same, relief.

(c) Rule in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 is liable to be discharged for failing to invoke or exhaust the alternative statutory remedy by way of appeal before the Press Appellate Board as provided under section 12A of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973.

(d) Rule in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 is also hit by the principle of res judicata inasmuch as the point involved in the present Rule has already been decided against the petitioners by the judgment passed in Writ Petition No. 1481 of 1994 and the petitioners did not challenge the same before the Appellate Division.

16. Apart from the aforesaid contentions regarding maintainability of the Rules, Mr Rafique- ul-Huq submits on merit thereof with good deal of force that clause (3) of Article 147 of the Constitution has created a bar for the persons appointed to or acting in the offices specified in clause (4) including a Minister to hold any office, post or position of profit or emolument or to take any part whatsoever in the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object. But the 'proviso' to clause (3) with a deeming clause has excluded the bar created by clause (3) from being applicable or operative against the office, post or position of profit or emolument which such persons held immediately prior to his appointment in the offices mentioned in clause (4) including the office of the Minister. In other words, it is contended by Mr Hoque, clause (3) of Article 147 should be read and construed along with the 'proviso' to mean that the persons holding the offices specified in clause (4) are debarred from being appointed in any office, post or position of profit or emolument and also from taking any part in the management or conduct of any such company, etc, but such person shall not be debarred from retaining his former office, post or position' of profit or emolument. Hence, according to Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, Mr Anwar Hossain has not lost his office as Executive Director-II in Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd and also his office, post or position as the Printer, Publisher and Editor of the Daily Ittefaq after he was appointed a Minister in the cabinet of General HM Ershad and during the coalition government of the Awami League.

17. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, in support of his aforesaid contention regarding maintainability of the writs, has cited a number of decisions from our as well as from the Indian jurisdiction. Particulars of some of them are as follows:

(1) 47 DLR 209 (2) 31 DLR (AD) 234 (3) 4 MLR (AD) 347 (4) 48 DLR 569 (5) 1998 BLD 363 (6) 6 MLR (AD) 8 (7) 45 DLR 260.

18. In the alternative, Mr Rafique-ul-Huq contends that Rules in all the writ petitions have now become infructuous as Mr Anwar Hossain was no longer a Minister. So, it would be futile exercise to hear the Rules as they had lost their efficacy by lapse of time, particularly when it involves consideration of constitutional provisions, which - are not liable to be decided merely as an academic issue. Mr Huq has relied upon a long line of decisions in this regard, some of which are as follows:

(1) AIR 1973 (SC) 87 (2) 1 BLC 229 (3) 43 DLR 179 (4) AIR 1960 (SC) 378.

19. In order to appreciate his arguments on the point of maintainability, I intend to examine the cases cited in this connection one by one.

20. In the case of Khurshed Alam vs Bangladesh; 47 DLR 209, question arose whether the writ petition challenging the decision of Election Appeal Board, created under the Election Rules framed under section 23 of the Trade Organisations Ordinance, 1961 was maintainable. It was held that the Election Appeal Board was a private body and not a local authority set up by any law nor does it perform any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic. In the circumstances writ petition was held not maintainable.

21. In the case of New Dhaka Industries Ltd vs Quamrul Huda and others, reported in 31 DLR (AD) 234, question arose whether an employee of New Dhaka Industries Ltd, incorporated under the Companies Act and subsequently nationalised under President's Order No. 27 of 1972, could challenge the order of dismissal passed by the management of the said company by filing writ petition against the said company. It was held that since New Dhaka Industries Ltd even after its nationalisation under the President's Order No. 27 of 1972 and vesting in the Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporation retained its corporate character, its employee Qumrul Huda could not invoke writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution in order to challenge his order of dismissal.

22. In the case of Md Abdur Rahman vs National Tea Company Ltd and others, reported in 4 MLR (AD) 347 it was held that since Md Abdur Rahman was an employee of National Tea Company Ltd and since National Tea Company was not a local authority within the meaning of section 3(28) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 the order of termination of his service by the Company was not liable to be challenged under the writ jurisdiction.

23. In the case of Jibon Kumar Barman vs M Abdul Hye. Chairman of the Election Committee and others reported in 48 DLR 569, question arose whether a member of a Matsajibi Samabaya Samity Ltd could maintain writ petition challenging rejection of his nomination paper and declaration of one Bachchu Bepari as elected uncontested. It was held that writ petition was not maintainable against the Members of the Election Committee of the Bangladesh Jatiyo Matsajibi Samabaya Samity Ltd as it was not a body or authority constituted or established by government under any law though it was registered as a Co-operative Society and was a body corporate under the Co-operative Society Ordinance 1984.

24. In the case of Sultana Nahar vs Bangladesh and others reported in 1998 BLD 363 = 2 BLC 430 hundreds of sex workers were evicted unlawfully. Writ was filed against the Government of Bangladesh and Others for same reliefs including direction to rehabilitate them. One of the learned Judges of the Division Bench discharged the Rule as not maintainable while the Rule was made absolute by the other Judge. The learned Judge while giving dissenting judgment stated that since the action done was not in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a legal authority it does not come under the mischief of Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. On a reference to the third Judge, the dissenting decision was upheld.

25. In the case of Md Abdur Rashid Khan vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, reported in 6 MLR (AD) 8, the writ petitioner Md Abdur Rashid Khan filed writ petition challenging the order of suspension from the post of principal of Barisal City College passed by the Deputy Commissioner, Barisal, as the Chairman of the Governing Body of the College. It was held in that case that "since the Deputy Commissioner passed the impugned order of suspension not as the Deputy Commissioner but as the Chairman of the Governing Body no writ lies as he was not performing the affairs of the Republic while passing the impugned order of suspension."

26. In the case of Shahabuddin (Md) vs Secretary, Ministry of Youth and Sports and others, reported in 45 DLR 360, the petitioner Shahabuddin General Secretary of Nabarun Sangsad, impugned the decision of one Syed Alamgir Faruk Chowdhury, passed by an Arbitration Tribunal, it was held that since these decisions including the decision passed by the Arbitration Tribunal were not taken by any person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority such decision cannot be called in question under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution.”

27. In the case of Manjurul Huq vs Bangladesh and others, reported in 44 DLR 239, the petitioner, a lessee of a Canteen of Diabetic Association, by filing writ petition prayed for a Rule Nisi under Article 102(2)(a) calling upon the Director General and the Secretary of the said Association to show cause as to why the orders passed by them requiring him to pay the arrear gas bills in connection with the canteen and the donation money due from him to the Association should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority. It was held that since the Bangladesh Diabetic Association is not a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority within the meaning of section 3(28) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 this Court under writ jurisdiction cannot give any direction to respondent Nos. 2-5 who are officers of the Bangladesh Diabetic Association.

28. In the case of Principal Abdul Ahad Choudhury vs Habibur Rahman and others, reported in 1995 BLD 124, the petitioner, Principal Abdul Ahad Choudhury as Chairman, Central Command Council, Bangladesh Muktijoddha Sangsad filed writ petition and obtained a Rule Nisi challenging some actions taken by respondent Nos. 1-8 towards holding of election of the said Sangsad. Rule in this case was discharged on the finding that the writ petition under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) was not maintainable as the respondent Nos. 1-8, although they were servants of the Republic of Bangladesh but were not functioning or doing any acts or deeds in connection with the affairs of the ,Republic nor they had acted in the affairs of the local authority as the Muktijoddha Sangsad was not a statutory body under any law.

29. In reply to the arguments on the point' of maintainability, the learned Counsels for the petitioners submits that since the acts challenged by these writ petitions were the acts of Mr Anwar Hossain to continue as the Executive Director-Il of the Company and as Printer, Publisher and Editor of the Daily Ittefaq while he was a Minister, such acts were alienable to writ jurisdiction under Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution, in other words, to invoke writ jurisdiction the acts impugned are required to be done by a person in the service of the Republic or a local authority but not required to be committed in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority.

30. On careful consideration of the decisions referred to above by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq on the point of maintainability, I find that the submissions made by Mr Huq have substance. I am therefore, led to hold that it is the act or omission which is done or committed in the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority and not just any other act is amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution. In Writ Petitions Nos. 3773 of 1996 and 3834 of 1999 the acts or deeds challenged were committed by Mr Anwar Hossain not in the affairs of the Republic or a local authority but in the affairs of Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd in his capacity as Executive Director-Il of the Company and as the Printer, Publisher and Editor of the Daily Ittefaq while he was a Minister. Hence the aforesaid writ petitions are not maintainable;

31. The learned Counsels for the petitioner also submits in the alternative that the impugned act of Mr Anwar Hossain to continue as the Executive Director-Il of the Company and also as the Printer, Publisher and Editor of the Daily Ittefaq is also violative of the fundamental right of press freedom under Article 39(1) of the Constitution and the writ petitions under reference should therefore be taken to have been filed under Article 102(1) for enforcement of the fundamental right. Hence Writ Petition No. 3773 of 1996 and Writ Petition No. 3834 of 1999 are maintainable inasmuch as the impugned act in breach of the fundamental right is not required to be committed in the affairs of the Republic or a local authority.

32. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, on the other hand, submits in reply that from the statements made in the aforesaid two writ petitions it cannot be said that the petitioner has been able to make out any case for enforcement of the fundamental right regarding press freedom. It cannot therefore be said that the writ petitions were filed under Article 102(1) of the Constitution for enforcement of fundamental right. No prayer has been made in these two writ petitions seeking enforcement of the fundamental right as is claimed now during the hearing for the petitioner. Moreover, even from the facts stated in these two writ petitions and the reliefs sought it cannot be said that the fundamental right by way of press freedom has been infringed by the impugned acts of Mr Anwar Hossain. This argument, it is submitted by Mr Huq, is but an act of desperation to bring in the violation of fundamental right only for the purpose of somehow making the Rules maintainable. This Court, therefore, should not be misled by such frivolous allegations on contravention of fundamental right. Mr Huq, in this connection, refers to the case of Mujibor Rahman (Md) vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111 and argues that such an argument of the learned Counsels, for the petitioners must be outright rejected.

33. The alternative argument advanced by Mr Akhtar Imam and Mr Abdur Rezzaque, the learned Counsels for the petitioners, that the aforesaid two Writ Petitions (WP No. 3773 of 1996 and WP No, 3834 of 1999) are maintainable as they should be taken to have been filed under Article 102 (1) of the Constitution for enforcement of the fundamental right concerning freedom of press does not appear to have any force and is not acceptable. In the case of Mujibor Rahman and others vs Bangladesh, 44 DLR (AD) 111, cited by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that an aggrieved person may, out of desperation or just for taking a sportive chance in the summary writ jurisdiction, allege contravention of some fundamental right which may turn out to be frivolous or vexatious or not even remotely attracted in his case. The Court is however, to be on guard so that the great value of the right given under Article 102(1) is not frittered away or misused as a substitute for more appropriate remedy available for an unlawful action involving no infringement of any fundamental right."

34. In the case of Khurshed Alam vs Bangladesh, 47 DLR 209, referred to above, their Lordships held in paragraph 12 of that judgment "We do not find any genuine plea for enforcement of fundamental right, rather Article 44 has been misquoted for the purpose."

35. I find force in the submissions made by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq. The aforesaid two writ petitions were neither directed nor they could be taken to have been filed for enforcement of any fundamental right of the petitioner including that of the freedom of press. The statements made in these two writ petitions, if considered in their proper perspective, do. not disclose any case of infringement of fundamental right, let alone the freedom of press. It appears tome that the arguments advanced in this connection by the learned Counsels of the petitioners is like a drowning man catching at a straw. The Writ Petitions Nos. 3773 of 1996 and 3834 of 1999 are also not maintainable on this account.

36. With regard to another branch of argument of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq regarding maintainability that the petitioners have also filed civil suits involving same points as in these three writ petitions and the Rules issued thereunder are not maintainable. Mr Akhtar Imam submits that pendency of civil suits does not always have the effect of rendering the Rules not maintainable or futile. I find substance in the submissions made by Mr Imam. In all these three writ petitions and the _ pending civil suits interpretation of Article 147(3) is involved. It therefore, appears that the point involved does not require determination of disputed questions of fact by taking evidence. The present writ petitions are therefore, more effective to resolve the point. The writ jurisdiction should not therefore be denied to the petitioners on the ground of pendency of civil suits. The case of Chairman, Civil Aviation Authority vs Kazi Abdur Rouf, 46 DLR (AD) 145, may be referred to in support ofthis view.

37. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq next submits that Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 is not maintainable inasmuch as the petitioners failed to invoke alternative statutory remedy by filing appeal before the Press Appellate Board under section 12A of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973. By elaborating his submissions, Mr Huq argues that the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka by the impugned letters dated 4-2-1997 and 3-4-1997, Annexures-E and G, in fact, refused to authenticate the declaration made by the petitioner No.1, Mr Mainul Hosein, by his letter dated 12-3-1997, Annexure-F, that Mr Rahat Khan was appointed as the editor in place of Mr Anwar Hossain since Mr Anwar Hossain ceased to be the editor in view of Article 147(3) of the Constitution after he became a Minister. Mr Nikhilesh Dutta, the learned Deputy Attorney- General, appearing for the respondent Nos. 1 and 2, adopted the arguments of Mr Huq in this case. The learned Counsels for the petitioners have however, dismissed the above arguments as misconceived and incorrect. It is submitted by the learned Counsels for the petitioners that the Additional District Magistrate illegally insisted by his aforesaid two impugned letters that Mr Anwar Hossain did not cease to be the Editor of the Daily Ittefaq even though he was appointed a Minister. It was therefore, not a case of refusal to authenticate a declaration and therefore, it was not necessary for the petitioner to file any appeal under section 12A. I find force in this contention of the learned Counsels for the petitioners and I am inclined to accept the same.

38. It is to be borne in mind that the question of alternative remedy is more a question of discretion and not a question of jurisdiction of the Court; AIR 1975 SC 1505 in the case of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd and another vs Assistant Collector of Customs and others, 1991 BLD (AD) 327, question arose in a customs matter where certain demands by the customs were challenged, whether application under Article 102 was maintainable without resorting to alternative statutory remady. It was held:

"In principle where an alternative remedy is available, an appl ication under Article 102 may not be entertained to circumvent a statutory procedure. There are, however, exceptions to the rule. Without attempting an exhaustive enumeration of all possible extraordinary situations we may note a few of them. In spite of an alternative statutory remedy, an aggrieved person may take recourse to Article 102 of the Constitution where the vires of the statute or a statutory provision is challenged, where the alternative remedy is not efficacious or adequate, and where the wrong complained of is so inextricably mixed up that the High Court Division may for the prevention of public injury and the vindication of public justice, examine that complaint. It is needless to add that the High Court Division is to see that the aggrieved person must have good reason for bypassing the remedy."

39. In view of what is stated above there was no necessity for the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 for filing any appeal under section 12A of said Printing Presses and Publications Act, 1973. Moreover, since interpretation of constitutional provision in Article 147(3) of the Constitution is involved in the matter I do not consider the appeal under section 12A of the said Act adequate and efficacious in this case. High Court Division in writ jurisdiction is a more effective forum in matters of interpretation of constitutional provision than the Press Appellate Board under section 12A.

40. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Counsel for the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain, also argues that even if these writ petitions under reference are held to be maintainable but the Rules issued therein have become infructuous for the reasons that Mr Anwar Hossain is no longer a Minister and Article 147(3) has no application now. Hence it would be a mere academic issue to determine the constitutional point whether Mr Anwar Hossain has ceased to be the Executive Director-Il of the Company and the printer, publisher and editor of the Daily lttefaq after he became a minister in the coalition government of the Awami League in view of Article 147(3) of the Constitution. Mr Huq cites some decisions in support of this contention. Now, I intend to discuss some of the authorities cited by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, in this regard.

41. In the case of M Saleem Ullah vs MdAbdur Rouf, Chief Election Commissioner and others reported in 1 BLC 229, Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause under what authority respondent No.1, Mr Justice Md Abdur Rouf, had been holding the office of the Judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh under Article 94 of the Constitution and also to show cause under what authority he was holding the office of the Chief Election Commissioner of Bangladesh under Artiele 118 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. It was held that since Mr Justice Md. Abdur Rouf returned to his earlier office as a Judge of the High Court Division and he was thereafter elevated to the Appellate Division as a Judge Rule did not subsist as it became infructuous.

42. In the case of Ghyas Siddique vs Bangladesh and others, 43 DLR 179. Rule was issued calling upon the Government in the Ministry of Home Affairs to show cause why the publications of future issues of the "Daily Millat" should not be declared illegal. During the pendency of the Rule the impugned order was withdrawn. In this circumstance it was held relying on the case of Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh, 33 DLR (AD) 201 that the Rule became infructuous. The relevant portion of the judgment in 33 DLR (AD) 201 delivered by K. Hossain CJ is as under:

"As regards the constitutionality of the section aforesaid we like to adhere to the well established self-set rule which says, the Court will not declare a law unconstitutional, if the case in which the question is raised can be properly disposed of in some other way."

43. In the case of State of Bihar vs Rai Bahadur Hurdat Roy Motilal Jute Mills and others, AIR 1960 SC 378, the Indian Supreme, Court observed:

"Any decision on the said question would, in such a case, be purely academic. Courts are and should be reluctant to decide constitutional points merely as matter of academic importance."

44. In the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh, 44 DLR (AD) 319 Mr Justice ATM Afzal, as he then was, observed as under:

"The Court does not answer merely academic questions but confines itself only to the point/points which are strictly necessary to be decided for the disposal of matter before it. This should be more so when constitutional questions are involved."

45. In the same case similar view was expressed by Latifur Rahman J, as he then was, stating-

"Abstract theoretical questions are not to be decided by any Court as those are only of academic importance."

46. The learned Counsels for the petitioner in reply submit that the principle to be borne in mind is, whether in the facts and circumstance of the case obligation is felt that the point or points involved in this case should still be answered even though it might appear that Rules had lost their efficacy. The learned Counsels contend with force that the mere fact that the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain is no longer a Minister did not render the constitutional issue involving the interpretation of Article 147(3) merely academic or useless. Because Mr Anwar Hossain still claims that he has not ceased to be the Executive Director-II in the Company and the Printer, Publisher and Editor of the Daily Ittefaq and, that since he is no longer a minister now, his name must appear in every day's issue of the Daily Ittefaq as editor in place of Mr Rahat Khan as he is the actual Editor and Mr Rahat Khan is merely acting as the acting editor during his absence. In this regard the learned Counsels refer to Annexure-X to the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner on 25-1-2003 showing that Mr Anwar Hossain by issuing the order dated 24-11-2002 (Annexure-X) insisted that his name should be published as the Editor. It is therefore, submitted that interpretation ofArtiele 147(3) is still necessary in spite of the fact that Mr Anwar Hossain is no more a Minister today. Unless this important question of law involving interpretation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution is settled, not only the premier daily itself will suffer a setback but also the people, namely, the readers of this premier daily, shall be deprived of the benefit of its publication as there exists a strong possibility that the publication might stop in future if this dispute is not settled in Court.

47. In the case of Himat Lal K Shah vs Commissioner of Police, Ahmedabad and others, AIR 1973 SC 87, there arose an important question as to the right of citizens in India to hold public meetings on public streets and the restriction which can be placed on that right. By the time the case was heard the two impugned orders had become infructuous by lapse of time. Despite this the High Court examined the other contentions raised before it, because it felt that the organisation of which the appellant was an office-bearer had to organise meetings on a number of occasions and every time the question of applying for permission would arise. In this view of the matter, the Court did not treat the Rules as infructuous altogether and decided the constitutional point involved in that case, namely, whether section 33(1) of the Bombay Police Act and the Rules framed thereunder were ultra vires Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Indian Constitution.

48. In the case of Haji Md Vakil vs Commissioner of Police, AIR 1954 Cal 159, cancellation of licence of firearm was challenged by filing writ and Rule was issued. In course of hearing of the Rule the learned Advocate General argued that even if the order of cancellation was bad no order should be made because the period for which the original licence was valid had expired and the application became infructuous. It was however held:

"It is true that it does not lie within the power of this Court to provide a fresh licence for the petitioner. But I do not agree with the proposition that the petitioner is not entitled to any relief. If the order of cancellation stands he is prejudiced in two ways, Firstly, there is the ignominy of a charge that the petitioner is guilty of something which is prejudicial to the security of public peace and secondly, his chances of procuring a fresh licence are greatly prejudiced if the cancellation of his licence is allowed to remain."

49. It appears from the cases cited above by the learned Counsels of both the sides that unless a decision is absolutely necessary the Court shall be slow to give any decision far less on a constitutional provision. It is again a question of discretion and not of jurisdiction of the Court. In an appropriate case, the Court may even pronounce on the constitutionality of statute even though it may not be necessary in that case. I am in agreement with the submissions made by the learned Counsels for the petitioners. The question whether Mr Anwar Hossain has ceased to be the Executive Director-II of the Company and the Printer, Publisher and the Editor of the Daily Ittefaq by operation of Article 147(3) after he accepted the office of a Minister is still required to be determined regardless of the fact that he is no longer a Minister. Because this dispute has been creating multiple problems not only in conducting the affairs of the Company but also in managing the day-to-day affairs of the Daily Ittefaq. In this view of the matter, the Rule in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 has not been infructuous.

50. Having held that Rule in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 has not become infructuous. I am now called upon to advert to and decide the core point namely, whether Mr Anwar Hossain has lost his office, post or position of Executive Director-II in the Company as well as the Printer, Publisher and Editor of the Daily Ittefaq in view of Article 147(3) after he became a Minister in the coalition government of the Awami League.

51. In the interest of clear understanding and proper appreciation of the arguments advanced on this point it is necessary to reiterate the same in brief. According to the learned Counsels for the petitioner, Mr Anwar Hossain has lost his office, post or position of the Executive Director-II in the Company and also of the Printer, Publisher and Editor of the Daily Ittefaq in view of Article 147(3) as soon as he took oath as a Minster and this loss or cessation of his aforesaid office, post or position is absolute and permanent and not temporary in the sense that such cessation of office, post or position continued till he continued as a Minister. The learned Counsels also contend that the 'proviso' to clause (3) declares that the offices specified in clause (4) of Article 147 are not offices of profit or emolument. On the other hand, Mr Rafique-ul-Huq contends that because of the 'proviso' to Article 147(3) a Minister or anyone holding or continuing in the office specified in clauses (4) of Article 147 can retain the office, post or position of profit or emolument in a company, association or a body having profit or gain as its object which he held immediately before he became Minister, etc. but he or they while continuing as a Minister, etc. shall be debarred from taking part in the administration or conduct of such company, etc. Mr Huq argues that this exception or relaxation is created by the framers of the Constitution with a view to utilising the services of capable, competent and qualified persons for the offices specified in clause (4) of Article 147.

52. In order to appreciate the arguments and reasoning advanced on the point I consider it advisable to reproduce the whole of Article 147 which reads as follows:

"147.(1) The remuneration, privileges and other terms and conditions of service of a person holding or acting in any office to which this Article applies shall be determined by or under an Act of Parliament but until they are so determined-

(a) they shall be those (if any) appertaining to the person holding or as the case may be acting in the office in question immediately before the commencement of this Constitution: or

(b) if the preceding sub-clause is applicable they shall be determined by order made by the President.

(2) The remuneration, privileges and other terms and conditions of service of a person holding or acting in any office to which this Article applies shall not be varied to the disadvantage of any such person during his term of office.

(3) No person appointed to or acting in an office to which this Article applies shall hold any office, post or position of profit or emolument or take any part whatsoever in 'the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object:

Provided that such person shall not for the purpose of this clause be deemed to hold any such office, post or position by reason only that he holds or is acting in the office first above-mentioned.

(4) This Article applies to the offices of, etc-

(a) President,

(b) Prime Minister or Chief Adviser,

(c) Speaker or Deputy Speaker,

(d) Minister, Adviser, Minister of State or Deputy Minister;

(e) Judge of the Supreme Court;

(i) Comptroller and Auditor General;

(g) Election Commissioner;

(h) Member of a public service commission"

53. It is well known that there are certain important differences in the theory of interpretation of a Constitution contrasted with the theory of interpretation of statutes. The interpretation of a Constitution involves more than a passing interest concerning the actual litigants and being a pronouncement of the Court on the government and administration, has a more general and far reaching consequence. I feel tempted to quote the Chief Justice Marshal of the American Supreme Court warning in McCulloch vs Maryland. 4 Wheaton 316 which runs as under:

"We must never forget that it is a Constitution we are expounding. The policy of a particular statute is more easily discernible and interpreted than the policy of a Constitution, which is a charter for government and administration of a whole nation and a country. It is that policy consideration which makes statutory interpretation different from interpretation of the Constitution. More foresight in the nature of judicial statesmanship, therefore, is required in interpreting a Constitution than in construing a statute. The Constitution is not to be construed in any narrow pedantic sense and a broad liberal spirit should inspire those whose duty it is to interpret it, for a Constitution, which provides for the Government of a country, is a living and organic thing, which of all instruments has the greatest claim to be construed ut res magis vailat quam pereat (it is better for a thing to have effect than to be made void). But this does not mean that a Court is free to stretch or pervert the language of a Constitution in the interest of any legal or constitutional theory, or even for the purpose of supplying omissions or for the purpose of correcting supposed errors."

54. In the case of Osman Gani Mandai vs Mainuddin Ahmed and others 27 DLR (AD) 61, second proviso to 7th paragraph of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution fell for interpretation and it was held," it is a cardinal rule of construction that where statutory restrictions are couched in negative terms they are almost invariably held to be mandatory". In the present case, we are called upon to interpret clause (3) of Article 147 along with its proviso.

55. A proviso to a section is not independent of the section calling for independent consideration or construction detached from the construction to be placed on the main section as it is merely subsidiary to the main section and is to be construed in the light of the section itself. The object of the proviso is to carve out from the main section a class or category to which the main section does not apply; and in so carving out the Court has always to bear in mind what is the class referred to in the section and must also remember that the carving out intended by the proviso is from the particular class dealt with by the main section and from no other class. The proviso can not possibly deal with an entirely different topic or subject and, it is subservient to the main provision; AIR 1966 SC 346. It is a cardinal rule of interpretation that is proviso to a particular provision of statute only embraces the field which is covered by main provision. It carves out an exception to the main provision to which it has been enacted as a proviso and to no other: Kanchanbhai vs Maneklal. AIR 1966 Guj 19. The general object of a proviso is to except something from the enacting clause or to qualify or restrain its generality and prevent misinterpretation. Ordinarily, a proviso to a section is intended to take out a part of the' main section for special treatment. The proviso is in the nature of an exception which takes a class out of the operation of the main section; Saradambal vs Seethalakshmi. AIR 1962 Mad 108.

56. Clause (3) of Article 147, couched in plain but negative language, has created an absolute bar for a person holding or acting in any of the offices specified in clause (4) of Article 147 to hold any office, post or position of profit or emolument or to take any part in the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object. Upon plain reading of clause (3) of Article 147 this bar cannot only be said to apply to any future engagement or appointment in such office, post or position but also to the office, post or position of profit or emolument which such person namely, the President, Prime Minister, Minister, Speaker, etc. held immediately before he was appointed as the President, Prime Minister. Minister Speaker, etc. as mentioned in clause (4) of Article 147. But by adding the proviso to clause (3)' of Article 147 the office, post or position of profit or emolument which such person held immediately before he was appointed the President. Prime Minister. Minister, Speaker, etc. is carved out and excluded from the operation of clause (3) of Article 147 keeping the bar in taking part in the management and conduct of the company, body or association intact. The purpose to except the aforesaid office, post or position from the operation of clause (3) of Article 147 has been achieved by inserting the deeming clause in the proviso. The words "such person" appearing in the first line of the proviso mean person holding or acting in any of the offices mentioned in clause (4) of Article 147 and the words "such office post or position" occurring in the second line of the proviso to clause (3) of Article 147 mean the office, post or position of profit or emolument in any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object. The contention that by the said 'proviso' the offices specified in clause (4) of Article 147 have been declared as offices without profit or emolument is not tenable. Because there 'has been no necessity in the entire Constitution warranting such declaration. Moreover, such construction does not also fit in with the context of clause (3) of Article 147. In the light of the aforesaid discussions. I hold that Mr Anwar Hossain has not ceased to be the Executive Director-II of the Company and the' Printer, Publisher and Editor of the Daily lttefaq for the reason that he was a Minister in the Government of HM Ershad and also in the coalition government of the Awami League.

57. Mr Razzaque, the learned Counsel for the petitioner, argues with some degree of vehemence that in all propriety the proviso to clause (3) of Article 147 of the Constitution must not be construed to allow the persons holding the offices in clause (4) to retain their prior office, post or position of profit or emolument as that would undermine the democratic values and norms and render our Constitution undemocratic. Because, unless a Minister divests himself of any financial interest on assuming office as a Minister that interest might give rise to conflict with his ministerial responsibilities. The learned Counsel, by making pointed reference to the English and Australian systems of parliament, submits that the Minister of these countries are subject to the rules for the registration and declaration of interests in addition to their being subject to guidelines and requirements laid down by successive Prime Ministers in order to ensure that no conflict arises or appears to arise between their private interests and public duties.

58. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq however, dismisses such argument as misplaced and irrelevant and submits that since the proviso to clause (3) of Article 147 permits such office, post or position to be retained by the President, Prime Minister, Minister, etc to hold otherwise would be an infraction of constitutional provision. I find good deal of force in the submission of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq. In the language of the Chief Justice Marshall, the Court is not free to stretch or pervert the language of the Constitution in the interest of any legal or constitutional theory, or even for the purpose of supplying omissions or for the purpose of correcting supposed errors in the Constitution. Ours is by far a democratic' Constitution. Bangladesh Constitution by inserting a proviso to clause (2) of Article 56 has allowed technocrats to be appointed Ministers even though they .are not Members of Parliament. This may appear to be undemocratic but not unconstitutional. Similarly, the provision of Non party Caretaker Government in Chapter IIA (Article 58B-58E) of the Constitution may also appear to be undemocratic. But these provisions have been incorporated in our Constitution in the recent past as a painful necessity.

59. It is contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Company, Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd, is in fact, the printer, publisher and editor of the Daily Ittefaq and Mr Anwar Hossain merely acted as such for the Company. Hence Mr Anwar Hossain was not competent to appoint Mr Rahat Khan as an acting editor of the Daily Ittefaq when he ceased to be the printer, publisher and editor. It therefore, fell for determination as a consequential issue, whether any artificial person can become the printer, publisher and editor of a newspaper.

60. From the scheme of the Presses and Publications Act, 1973 and also from the language employed in section 2(k), 2(m) and section 7 of the said Act, 1973, it is clear that not only a natural person but also an artificial person, like a company, can become a printer and a publisher ofa newspaper in Bangladesh. Expressions used in section 7 more clearly support this position, which are as follows:

"The printer and the publisher of every newspaper shall appear, in person or by agent before the District Magistrate and shall make and subscribe, in duplicate originals, a declaration in Form B."

61. Where a company is the printer and publisher, such company shall authorise a natural person by a resolution adopted by its board of directors to discharge the functions of the printer and publisher on its behalf. In the present case, the Company (lttefaq Group of Publications Ltd) is the printer and publisher of the Daily Ittefaq and Mr Anwar Hossain is appointed by the Company pursuant to 11 resolution adopted by its board of directors to act on behalf of the Company as the printer and publisher. The declaration made by Mr Anwar Hossain in Form B on 21-4-85 confirms and also conforms to this position.

62. But with regard to the editor of a newspaper the position in law is different. The Printing Presses and Publications Act, 1973 does not contemplate any artificial person to become the editor of a newspaper. This position is implicit in the definition of Editor given under section 2(d) and section 12(2)(h) of the said Act which reads as under:

"Section 2(d) "editor" means the person who controls the selection of the matter that is published in a newspaper." "Section 12(2)(h) the editor possesses reasonable educational qualifications or has had adequate training or experience in journalism."

63. The very nature of the powers and functions to be exercised and discharged by the editor of a newspaper requires exercise of human intelligence and discretion. Mr Anwar Hossain was appointed as the Editor-of the Daily Ittefaq by a resolution of the Company in 1972. Subsequently, he was also made the printer and publisher of the said daily by a resolution dated 30-5-85 of the Company.

64. Since 1 have already held that the post and position of Mr Anwar Hossain as the editor of the Daily Ittefaq remained unaffected even after his appointment as Minister there was no necessity for the Company (Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd) to appoint any other person as the editor. During the period when Mr Anwar Hossain was a Minister and was debarred from performing functions as editor the Company, as the real printer and publisher, was required to appoint someone as the acting editor. In this case, Mr Anwar Hossain appointed Mr Rahat Khan as the acting editor and communicated this position to the District Magistrate. Since the Company by any resolution did not disapprove the appointment of Mr Rahat Khan as the acting editor, such appointment should be taken to have been concurred or made by the Company. To construe otherwise will create a void in the administration and must therefore be avoided. The District Magistrate, or for that matter, the Additional District Magistrate having approved and acted upon such appointment did not commit any illegality by issuing impugned letters, Annexures E and G to the Writ petition.

65. The Presses and Publications Act, 1973 does not require any formal declaration and authentication under sections 7 and 12 of the said Act in case of change of the editor. Such declaration and authentication is necessary only in case of any change of the printer and publisher or in case of change of language, periodicity or place of publication. The contention of the learned Counsels of the petitioners in this regard is therefore, not tenable in law and is rejected.

66. In the result, the Rules in all the writ petitions are discharged for the above reasons without any order as to costs.

Unless extremely necessary: I shall not repeat facts that have been stated by my Lord in the main judgment and the citations already discussed.

68. In these Write Petitions it is imperative to interpret Articles 102, 147(3)(4) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the Articles relating to fundamental rights of the petitioners together with the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and' Registration) Act, 1973 and Freedom of Press for proper consideration of facts-in-issue and disposal of the Writ petitions on their merits.

69. For the purpose of discussion and conclusion I shall recapitulate the arguments advanced by both the parties in support of their respective cases.

70. Relying upon Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh Mr Akhtar Imam, Learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain as soon as he entered upon the office of a Minister on 23rd June, 1996 the said Article Came into play on him and by operation of this Article he lost all offices of profit disqualifying himself further to take any part in the management and conduct of those offices. According to him, the posts of Editor, Printer and Publisher in the Daily Ittefaq and the post of Executive Director-II in the Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd are all posts of profit. Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited provide that the object of the Company amongst others, was to make profit by running the going concerns namely, the New Nation Printing Press, the Daily Ittefaq, the weekly Purbani and the weekly Dhaka Times and, as such, these posts carrying emoluments are posts of profit. Mr Anwar Hossain therefore, lost these posts ipso facto on 23rd June, 1996 by operation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution. Since clause (3) of Article 147 provides that the persons to whom this Article applies shall not hold any office, post or position of profit or emolument or take any part whatsoever in the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object, and clause (4) of the said Article provides that the Article applies to the offices of (a) President; (b) Prime Minister or the Chief Adviser: (c) Speaker or Deputy Speaker: (d) Minister or Adviser, Minister of State or Deputy Minister; (e) Judge of the Supreme Court; (i) Comptroller and Auditor General; (g) Election Commissioner: (h) Member of the Public Service Commission: the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain being a Minister was incapable of taking any part whatsoever in the management or conduct of the company named the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited and thus his actions appointing Mr Rahat Khan as Editor-in- charge of the Daily Ittefaq, which is one of the subject matters of Writ Petition No. 3773 of 1996, and order of re-instatement of Mr Monowarul Islam, Chief Accountant on 25-9-1999, suspension order of Md Habibullah, the Senior Security Officer of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd dated 23-1-1999 and order of appointment of Mr Shawkat Hossain Masum as in-charge of Finance Page of the Daily Ittefaq dated 17-8-1999 and subsequent cancellations of those orders by this respondent on 19-2-2000 which are subject matters of Writ Petition No. 3834 of 1999, are all ilIegal, void, without jurisdiction and malafide, for at the time of issuing those orders and cancellations thereof the respondent was holding the office of a Minister and has illegally and in violation of Constitutional provisions taken part in the management and conduct of the Company.

71. According to Mr Imam, the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain by entering upon the office of a Minister has incurred two-fold disqualifications, viz (i) He lost the post and office of the Editor in the Daily Ittefaq and the posts and offices of Executive Director-II, Printer and Publisher in the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited, and (ii) disqualified himself to take any part whatsoever in the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object during his tenure as a Minister, that is to say, the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited and the Daily Ittefaq.

72. Article 147 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has been quoted in the main Judgment.

73. Mr Akhtar Imam, the learned Advocate, next argued that by virtue of proviso to clause (3) of Article 147, the office of a Minister, as such, shall not be an office of profit and the respondent was not debarred from receiving financial benefits attached to the office of a Minister while he was holding the post and position of a Minister. This clause (3) and its proviso, therefore, disabled the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain to hold any office in the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited, on the one hand and qualified him to receive all his financial benefits attached to the office of a Minister, on the other.

74. The second branch of argument of Mr Akhtar Imam is that the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka, respondent No.2 in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 has acted illegally, firstly, by issuing a letter addressing the respondent No.3, Mr Anwar Hossain as Publisher of the Daily Ittefaq on 4-2-1997 stating that his office had no objection to the appointment of Mr Rahat Khan as Editor-in- charge of the Daily Ittefaq (Annexure-E) during his absence as Editor, and secondly, by writing a letter to the petitioner Mr Mainul Hossain on 3-4-1997 in response to his objection (Annexure-F), asserting that Mr Anwar Hossain is still the Printer and Publisher of the Daily Ittefaq and it is the Publisher who alone shall decide by whom he shall edit the newspaper vide Annexure-G and thirdly, by not saying that Mr Anwar Hossain made the Declaration on behalf of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd which appears from the Declaration itself and also by not holding that the lttefaq Group of Publications Ltd is the real Printer and Publisher of the Daily lttefaq.

75. Mr Imam has vehemently argued that the stand taken by the Additional District Magistrate. Dhaka is not only erroneous and biased but arrogant and malafide, for, in the Declaration itself that was given by the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain under section 7 of the Printing Presses and Publication (Declaration and Registration) Act 1973. Annexure- D to WP No. 2746 of 1997 pursuant to a Resolution (Annexure-C) to WP No. 2746 of 1997 of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd following the resignation of former Printer and Publisher Mr Motahar Hossain Siddiqui, contained a line saying that he was making the declaration on behalf of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited and, as such, the Company is the real Printer and Publisher of the Daily Ittefaq and Mr Anwar Hossain was mere a human agent of the company like his predecessor Mr Motahar Hossain Siddiqui who was an officer of the Company  and not even a shareholder, The Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka has deliberately ignored the real Printer and Publisher (the Company) of the Daily Ittefaq and held the agent to be the Printer and Publisher and deliberately violating all norms arrogantly said that matter of appointment of Editor of the Daily Ittefaq is the wish of Mr Anwar Hossain, the Publisher. The Additional District Magistrate was not competent to write impugned Annexure-G in response to the letter of Mr Mainul Hosein and those are without jurisdiction, void, malafide and are of no legal effect. Mr Imam has contended that 'person' contemplated in various sections of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act. 1973 includes a 'juristic person'.

76. In support of his contentions, Mr Akhtar Imam had relied upon the cases of Motahar Hossain Siddiqui vs Bangladesh, reported in 33 DLR 238, Shahid Nabi Malik vs Chief Election Commissioner and others PLD 1997 (SC) 32. Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir and others vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 319, M Saleem Ullah, Advocate vs Justice Mohammad Abdul Quddus Chowdhury and another, reported in 46 DLR 691, an unreported Judgment in the case of Mainul Hosein vs Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others in Writ Petition No. 1481 of 1994.

77. Mr Abdur Razzaque, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner in Writ Petition No.2746 of 1997 while adopting submissions of Mr Akhtar Imam added that clause (3) of Article 147 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has two parts: (1) A Minister shall not hold any office, post and position other than the post and office of the Minister; and (2) this disqualification is complete cessation and not mere suspension. According to him, had the clause (3) of Article 147 contemplated a temporary suspension to say, that a Minster is disqualified to hold any office of profit during his tenure only, the framers of the Constitution would have used the words "during that time" after the provisions of Article 147 (3) as is the case of the House of Commons (Disqualification) Act, 1781. 95. Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh reads as follows:

"(1) The High Court Division, on the application of any person aggrieved, may give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic, as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of this Constitution.

(2) The High Court Division may, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law

(a) on the application of any person aggrieved make an order

(i) directing a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by  law to do or

(ii) declaring that any act done or proceeding taken by a person perform ing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect, or

(b) on the application of any person, make an order

(i) directing that a person in custody be brought before it so that it may satisfy itself that he is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner; or

(ii) requiring a person holding or purporting to hold a public office to show under what authority he claims to hold that office.

(5) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires. "person" includes a statutory public authority and any Court or tribunal other than a Court or tribunal established under a law relating to the defence services of Bangladesh or any disciplined force or a tribunal to which Article 117 applies."

96. Article 102 is the continuation of Article 44(1) which provides. "The right to move the High Court Division in accordance with clause (1) of Article 102 for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this part is guaranteed."

97. The corresponding analogous Article in the Constitution is Article 32 that guaranteed the right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III. But Article 32 of the Indian Constitution is wider in scope inasmuch as Clause (4) of Article 32 is concerned. Clause (4) provides that:

"(4) The right guaranteed by this Article shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution."

98. According to clause (1) of Article 102, for the purpose of enforcement of any of the fundamental rights the High Court Division on an application of any person aggrieved may give such directions or orders to any person or authority.

99. The Article then adds "including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic," as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution.

100. There are two categories in this Article to whom the High Court Division may give directions or Orders. In the 1 st category, to any person or authority, and in the 2nd category,including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic.

101. Clause (5) of this Article provides that person shall include a statutory public authority, any Court or tribunal.

102. In the interpreting Article 152 of the Constitution there are no definitions of Person or Authority.

General Clause Act, 1897 in its section 3(39) has defined "Person". "Person" shall include any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not."

103. In this definition too the term, "Person" has not been defined but provides what person shall include Inclusion in essence is addition. Person is an entity and according to this defining clause, an entity of person, in addition, shall include any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not.

104. John Salmon in his Jurisprudence (Granville L Williams, 10th Edition, 1947, page- 318) has defined the term Person as follows: "So far as Legal theory is concerned, a person is any being whom the law regards as capable of rights and duties. Any being that is not so capable is a person, whether a human being or not and not being that is not so capable is a person even though he be a man. Persons are the substances of which rights and duties are the attributes. It is only in this respect that persons possess judicial significance, and this is the exclusive point of view from which personality receives Legal recognition."

But is the District Magistrate, Dhaka or for that matter, a Minister of the People's Republic of Bangladesh a person? Of course, rights and duties are attributed to both of them. Here the term 'authority' is relevant. Both the Constitution and the General Clauses Act have not defined the term authority. The Dictionary meaning of the term authority is "Power or right to enforce obedience; delegated power; person or body having authority; personal influence (The Concise Oxford Dictionary, 7th edition)."
