"A definition of the term Minister is given in Wharton's Law Lexicon (Sweet and Maxwell, 4th edition) "Minister is One to whom sovereign entrusts the Administration. In Great Britain, the word ministry is used as a collective noun for the heads of departments in the state forming the Government and responsible to the Parliament."

109. In the Parliamentary Democratic System of Government in Bangladesh the concept is almost the same. The Administration is entrusted to a Minister by the President in exercise of his sovereign power on the advice of the Head of the Government, namely, the Prime Minister.

110. Though the Minister and the District Magistrate are authority within the meaning of the Constitution here is the line of demarcation and this is, a District Magistrate is in the service of the Republic but the Minister is not. He is head of the administration of his Ministry performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic. While the job of a person in the service of the Republic is arising out and out of service to the pleasure of the President, a Minister's job is an entrustment placed upon him by the sovereign. The Minister is jointly as a Cabinet and severally as a Ministerial head responsible to the Parliament. A person in the service of the republic is responsible to his appointing authority. A person in the service of the Republic is therefore, responsible to a Minister and a Minister is responsible to the people through the people's representatives. Service in the Republic is depended upon the Pleasure of the President also manifested in different statutes and the tenure of the Minister is dependent upon Pleasure of the People manifested in general elections, for, all powers in the Republic belong to the people (Article 7 of the Constitution).

111. The tenure of a Minister is often a subject of discussion among the Jurists. Some say, the tenure of a Minister is during the pleasure of the Prime Minister and temporary in nature. This logic is founded on the Article 58(2) which provides that the Prime Minister may at any time request a Minister to resign and if such Minister fails to comply with the request, may advise the President to terminate the appointment of such Minister. It is more so, when tenure of other office holders are taken into consideration. The term of office of the President is five years (Article 50), the tenure of the Attorney-General is during pleasure of the President (Article 64(4), the term of the Parliament is five years (Article 70(3) the tenure of a Judge of the Supreme Court is 65 years, the term of an Election Commissioner is five year (Article 118(3), the tenure of the Auditor General is sixty years (Article 129(1), the terms of office of the Chairman and other members of the Public Service Commission are five years (Article 139). But the Articles relating to the Prime Minister and the Cabinet Ministers and tenure of office of Prime Minister, other Ministers namely, the Articles 55, 56, 57 and 58 do not specifically provide any time limit of office. Article 57 provides that the office of the Prime Minister shall become vacant ifhe resigns from the office or ceases to be a member of Parliament. Article 58 provides that an office of a Minister shall become vacant if he resigns from the office, ceases to be a members of Parliament if the President directs under clause (2) or if the Prime Minister resigns from or ceases to hold office. Article 57 and 58 enumerate the circumstances when the office of the Prime Minister and other Ministers shall become vacant. If these circumstances and contingency do not occur then there must be a term of office for the Prime Minister and the Ministers which has categorically not been mentioned in these two Articles like Article 50 of the Constitution. But the same is there in the framework of the Constitution. Under Article 56(3) the President shall appoint a member of Parliament as Prime Minister who commands the support of the majority of the members of the Parliament. The Prime Minister shall determine number of Ministers nine-tenth of whom shall be appointed from among members of the Parliament and the Parliament under Article 72(3) shall stand dissolved on the expiration of the period of five years unless sooner dissolved by the President. As such, term of office of the Prime Minister and the Ministers are the term of the Parliament i-e five years. Of course on the pleasure of the Prime Minister an individual Minister must vacate his ministerial office but another individual to the choice of the Prime Minister shall come to occupy the office and the Minister will remain there in the office irrespective of change of person. Tenure of a Minister is not the tenure of a person but of the office and, as such, though a person may retain or vacate his office on the pleasure of the Prime Minister but the office of the Minister remains for five years and, as such, this office is not temporary in nature. There is no reason to say that the office of the President is temporary in nature only because its tenure is five years. So also, the office of the Election Commissioner or the Chairman and Members of the Public Service Commission. It is the nature and character of the office.

112. However, both the Minister and the District Magistrate again, perform functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic one being the head of the department and the other being subordinate in the Administration. The former being controlling authority and the latter subordinate authority. They both are 'authority' in their  respective realm and to both the High Court Division may give any directions and orders as may be appropriate.

113. An aggrieved person can, therefore, maintain a Writ Petition against both of them jointly or severally. In this perspective 'person' and authority are genus while the term 'person' performing function in connection with the affairs of the Republic or a local authority are species. This person performing function is in addition to and not derogation of 'person' and 'authority' as envisaged in Article 102(1) of the Constitution.

If any Minister by his acts, omissions or conduct violates or offends any of the Constitutional provisions with impunity and any person is aggrieved thereby, that person can maintain a Writ Petition against such violative acts, activities or actions. Minister being the administrative head having power, authority and personal influence those are always under judicial scrutiny.

Placing reliance upon the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir; the learned Advocate for the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain submits that the Appellate Division, in this case, has held that "The Court does not answer merely academic question but confines itself only to the point/points which are strictly necessary to be decided for the disposal of the matter before it. This should be more so when Constitutional questions are involved" and that "abstract theoretical questions are not to be decided by any Court as those are of only academic importance."

120. Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir challenged the Constitutional validity of the Local Government (Upazila Parishad and Upazila Administration Reorganisation) (Repeal) Ordinance, 1991 on the ground that this' Ordinance was inconsistent with Articles 9, 11, 59 and 60 of the Constitution and, as such; it was void in terms of Articles 7(2) of the Constitution. During hearing their Lordships found that the repeal Ordinance was no more in existence which has been made an Act being Act No.2 of 1992.

Paragraphs 58 and 59 of that Judgment maybe quoted to appreciate why their Lordships held that the Court does not answer to merely academic questions and what academic questions really are:

"58 Naimuddin J in his Judgment found that the Upazila Parishad was not a local Government institution within the meaning of Articles 59 and 9 of the Constitution and, as such, Article 9 cannot be invoked for declaring the repealing Ordinance Act void under 7(2) on the ground of inconsistency with Article 9. He has not also found that the impugned Ordinance/Act is in conflict with any other provision of Part II of the Constitution containing Fundamental Principles of State Policy. That being so it was wholly unnecessary to decide whether in view of the Provision in sub-article (2) of Article 8 that the principles set out in Part II shall not be judicially enforceable, any legislative act which is in direct conflict with and passed in flagrant violation of the provisions of Part II can be declared void under Article 7(2). Having answered this hypothetical question in the affirmative after taking hypothetical facts into consideration in a lengthy discussion the learned Judge addressed himself to the real question thus:

"Consequently, if it is found that the impugned repealing Ordinance is violative of Article 9 of the Constitution it is liable to be struck down as void in view of Article 7(2) of the Constitution."

"59 Then the finding was made that the repealing Ordinance was not violative of Article 9 with which we have agreed. Therefore, the broad decision that a law can be declared void in case of a conflict with any provision of Part II of the Constitution was uncalled for and made on hypothetical facts. This, as a rule, the Court always abhors. The Court does not answer merely academic question but confines itself only to the point/points which are strictly necessary to be decided for the disposal of the matter before it. This should be more so when constitutional questions are involved and the Court should be ever discreet in such matters. Unlike a civil suit the practice in constitutional cases has always been that if the matter can be decided by deciding one issue only no other point need be decided."

121. Mr Akhtar Imam has cited a case from Indian Jurisdiction in this respect. In the case of Madhu Limaye vs Superintendent, Tihar Jail, Delhi, reported in AIR 1975 (SC) 1505, the petitioner Shri Madhu Limaye, MP moved the petition against the Rules in Jail Manual making discrimination between European and Indian prisoners. The Solicitor General raised objection that the petitioner having been freed from prison years ago this Court should not be invited into an academic exercise on a constitutional issue. The Learned Court observed, "Mr Santok Singh for the petitioner has brought to our notice decisions of this Court and of the Supreme Court of the United States to press home his point that issues of such great moment affecting the liberty of citizen should not be avoided even though the immediate prohibition which has led to the WP has for the time being disappeared." The Learned Court then held that "the petitioner is no longer in prison. Even so, may be the matter can be competently scrutinised from the Constitutional angle by this Court." Their Lordships, in this case, have further held that "It is question of discretion and not of Jurisdiction of the Court."

122. The case of Uttara Jute Fibres Industries has been cited by the Learned Advocate for the respondent in support of his arguments that the High Court Division exercising constitutional Jurisdiction should not enter into company matters. According to him, the subject matters of these three Writ Petitions are out and out company matters of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd and this Court while exercising Writ Jurisdictions must not enter into the Company matters.

123. BRTC filed an application before the Learned Company Judge of the High Court Division praying for winding up of the Company, namely, Ms Ashraf Jute Mills Ltd for arrear rent. The petition was allowed and the learned Court appointed the official receiver of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh as the official liquidator of the said Company in liquidation. But in the meantime the BSRS had sold out the Mills to a third party to recover its outstanding loan from the Company. The official liquidator took possession of the office of the Company situated at BRTC Bhaban, issued several notices upon the Managing Director of the Rupali Bank to hand over possession of the goods, raw jute and machineries and other immovable properties which were in possession of the Bank as mortgagee and the official liquidator reported that the properties of the Jute Mills had been sold during the pendency of the liquidation proceeding without the order of the Court and that the sale was fraudulent and illegal. The learned Company Judge issued a Rule calling upon the BSRS and the purchaser to show cause why the sale dated 17-1-90 of the Ashraf Jute Mills Ltd in liquidation should not be cancelled, set aside and why they should not be directed to deliver all the properties, both movable and immovable, of Ashraf Jute Mills Ltd to the official liquidator.

124. The Learned Company Judge after hearing the parties made the Rule absolute by Judgment and Order dated 28-8-91 declaring the sale dated 17-1-90 as illegal and void and consequently, set aside the sale holding, amongst others, that clause (5) of Article 34 of the BSRS Order does not bar the Supreme Court of Bangladesh from interfering with the sale held under Article 34 and that there were elements of fraud, recklessness and malafide motive of the BSRS when it exercised its power arbitrarily ignoring the pending proceeding before the High Court Division.

125. Against this Judgment the two appeals arose where Mr Rafique-ul-Huq has appeared for the appellant purchaser of the Mills, Uttara Jute Fibres taking the plea of bonafide purchaser and argued that the Learned Company. Judge while exercising Jurisdiction under the Companies Act, has erred in law in setting aside the sale, for the Learned Company Judge was not exercising his Jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. In this background their Lordships held that "Thus we are of the opinion that' matters decided under the Companies Act in the High Court Division are not under the Constitutional Jurisdiction of the High Court Division but under a Special Statutory Jurisdiction conferred upon the High Court Division by the Companies Act itself."

126. In the case of M Salimullah vs Justice Mohammad Abdur Rouf, reported in 1 BLC 227 their Lordships found that "neither the office of the Judge and nor that of Chief Election Commissioner is an office of profit or emolument as contemplated under clause (3) of Article 147 and that the office of the persons enumerated in Article 147(3) have been clearly distinguished from the office of persons enumerated in Article 147(4) and, for that matter, from the office of persons in the service of the Republic."

127. This decision, to my view, rather supports the contention of Mr Akhtar Imam and Mr Abdur Razzaque that the offices specified in clause (4) are not offices of profit and the proviso to clause (3) have kept these offices out of the ambit of clause (3).

128. In the case of Ghyas Siddique vs Bangladesh, reported in 43 DLR 179 publication of future issues .of 'Daily Millat' was prohibited under section 17(1)(c) of the Special Powers Act. 1974 on 12-12-89. During hearing of the matter Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, Learned Advocate, took an adjournment for filing Government Order withdrawing and rescinding the Order dated 12-12-89 and a Government Order dated 17-4-90 was annexed showing that the Government has withdrawn the Order dated 12-12-89. Under this circumstances the Government, relying upon the case of Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh, Supra, prayed for discharge of the Rule being infructuous and the Learned Court held that "in view of the aforesaid Annexures filed by the respondent (Annexure-I and Annexure-1/1) the Rule has become infructuous. 'The petitioner also does not want to proceed with the Rule' as it has become infructuous in view of the rescinding of the impugned Order by the Government."

129. In the Supplementary Affidavit-in-opposition sworn in on 14-12-2000 in Writ Petition No.2746 of 1997. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq has referred to a case reported in 4 BLC (AD) 114. This is a case of Mridul Kanti Chowdhury vs Chittagong Steel Mills Ltd where pay scale of some, Senior Assistants was the fact in issue. They got promotion from 13th grade to 12th grade and the Labour Court ordered to give them pay scale of 11th grade. The Learned Judges of the High Court Division found the Order of the Labour Court was without authority and the Appellate Division dismissed their Leave Petition.

130. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq has also referred to in his another Supplementary Affidavit-in-opposition the case of Shahajadi Begum Waqf Estate vs Secretary, Ministry of Communication & another reported in 7 BLC (AD) 41 where it was found that during pendency of suits on the self-same matter petitioner tried to invoke writ Jurisdiction and was refused.

131. In the case of the State of Bihar vs RBHRM Jute Mills reported in AIR 1960 (SC) 378 the question arose as to whether proviso to section 14A of the Bihar Sales Tax Act (19 of 1974) was applied to that case for the Solicitor-General pressed the preliminary point that the proviso was not applicable in that case. The Learned Court then observed that "We would therefore, first deal with this preliminary point. In cases where the vires of statutory provisions are challenged on constitutional grounds, it is essential that the material facts should first be clarified and ascertained with a view to determine whether the impugned statutory provisions are attracted, if they are, the constitutional challenge on their validity must be examined and decided. If however, the facts admitted or proved do not attract the impugned provisions there is no occasion to decide the issue about the vires of the said provisions. Any decision on the said question would in such a case be purely academic."

132. I shall advert to other citations of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq but on discussion of the cases relied upon on the point of maintainability, I find that facts and circumstances of those cases including those discussed by my Lord in the main judgment are distinguishable from those of the instant three Writ Petitions and are not applicable in the given facts and circumstances.

133. Mr Akhtar Imam, on the other hand, has placed. his reliance upon the cases of BC and Company vs Union of India reported in AIR 1973 (SC) 107 and Bangladesh vs Syed Chand Sultana and others reported in 51 DLR (AD) 24 in support of his contentions that the Writ Petitions are maintainable when the actions taken are found to be ex facie illegal and if for argument's sake the Rules have become infructuous but still the Learned Court may decide the issues raised relating to Articles 102 and 147(3) and other grounds of violation of fundamental rights envisaged in Articles 27, 32, 39 and 40 of the Constitution and as well as sections 5, 7, 12, 16 and 20 of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act. 1973 and that the alternative forum is not a bar if it does not provide equally efficacious remedy.

134. In the case of BC and Company vs Union of India question arose-Merely because the petitioner is a Company owning and publishing newspapers whether its shareholders, editors, printers and directors are debarred from invoking their fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(a).

"Article 19(1 )(a) is relating to Press Freedom in the Indian Constitution. It was held in that case that "The fundamental rights of shareholders as citizens are not lost when they associate to form a company. When their fundamental rights as shareholders are impaired by state action their rights as shareholders are protected. The reason is that the shareholders' rights are equally and necessarily affected if the rights of the company are affected. "II was also held that," Liberty of the press is an essential part of the press freedom, speech and expression and that Freedom of Press does not mean freedom of the owner of the press but freedom of the readers of the newspaper."

135. In these three Writ Petitions allegations are that after becoming a 'Minister the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain has impaired the Press Freedom by exerting his ministerial powers, authority and position interfering in the management and conduct of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited and the Daily Ittefaq to the prejudice to its directors shareholders and readers at large.

136. In the decision given in the case of Bangladesh vs Md Azizur Rahman & others Supra their Lordships held that "If found from the facts of the Writ Petitions that the question of fundamental right invoked therein has been so mixed up with the facts and statutory rules that the question of fundamental right cannot be extricated for exclusive consideration in a petition for enforcement of fundamental right the Writ Petition is maintainable."

137. In the instant three Writ Petitions facts are so interwoven with different sections of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 and with the fundamental rights of the petitioner and the company together with the press freedom and mandatory Constitutional provisions, I find these three Writ Petitions are maintainable. Matters relating to violation of any provision of the Constitution or Statute are not matters relating to the business or affairs of the Company and, as such, Article 85 of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited or section 233 of the Companies Act have no manner of application in these Writ Petitions under the given facts and circumstances.

138. Rules in these three Writ Petitions are therefore not infructuous.

139. In the case of Syeda Chand Sultana referred to above, the question of alternative forum and alternative remedy arose. The same questions arose in many other cases viz. Dhaka Warehouse Ltd vs Assistant Collector, Customs. 1991 BLD (AD) 227, Sarwari Begum vs Bangladesh. 45 DLR 571, Dhaka University vs Md Mohiuddin, 44 DLR (AD) 305, MA Hai vs TCB, 40 DLR (AD) 206, etc. and it was found that ceremonial exercise of alternative forum was not necessary when action ex- facie void for want of jurisdiction where fundamental rights of the petitioner have apparently found to be violated if he is a person aggrieved or the question raised is purely a question of law or interpretation of statute.

140. In the case of Rafiqul Hoque vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR 398 it was held that alternative forum was not a bar for granting relief under Article 102(1) but a bar under Article 102(2). In a recent case, Bangladesh vs Mizanur Rahman reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149 their Lordships held that "When a Writ Petition is filed for enforcement of fundamental right under Article 102(1) of the Constitution there is no question of exhaustion of other equally efficacious remedy and, as such, in spite of such remedy being available in the matter under any law a Writ Petition for enforcement of any of the fundamental rights appears to be maintainable."

141. The petitioner went to the Press Council and the Press Council by resolution dated 24-3-1994 has restrained the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain from publishing his name as Editor of the Daily Ittefaq. The respondent has tiled a Writ Petition being No. 1008 of 1994 against the resolution of the Press Council but did not proceed further and the Press Council's decision prevailed. To ask the petitioner to go to the Press Council again for interpretation of sections 7, 12, 16 or 20 of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 and Article 147(3) of the Constitution is .nothing but 'ceremonial exercise' which I find was not necessary in the facts and circumstances of these three Writ Petitions. Moreover, I find that the Press Appellate Board introduced by Act VIII of 1991 has no jurisdiction to deal with these types of questions.

142. In Writ Petition No.1481 of 1994 their Lordships while considering as to whether a fresh Declaration was necessary on the part of the respondent eventually found that "the respondent No.3 was holding the office of the Minister also continued to print his name as Printer and Publisher of the "Daily Inefaq" which leads to show participation in the management and conduct in the business of the affairs of the Company having profit or gain", and observed that "the respondent No.1 (the District Magistrate, Dhaka) having being notified earlier by the petitioner through his letter dated 21-1-92 evidenced by Annexure-F (to that Writ Petition) ought to have taken notice of the fact that the respondent No.3 was holding the office of printer and publisher as well as the office of the Minister simultaneously and hence ought to have enquired into the matter and examine as to whether there was any violation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution at all and thus the respondent No.1 failed to see that the 'Daily Ittefaq' is not published with the disqualified person."

143. Their Lordships have further held that "the issue of the constitutional bar, as contemplated by Article 147(3) has to be initially examined and decided by the respondent No.1 if such point is raised before him in accordance with law which in the instant case requires scrutiny of the resolutions taken by the Company and the law relating to the principle of estoppel."

144. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq has argued that this judgment constitutes res judicata. In the main judgment my Lord had found that principle of res judicata is not applicable in these cases. It appears that the petitioner by Annexure-F to the Writ Petition No.2746 of 1997 brought these matters to the notice/knowledge of the District Magistrate and the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka and the latter by Annexure-G has outright rejected his objections holding that Mr Anwar Hossain is the Printer and Publisher of the Daily Ittefaq by virtue of Declaration dated 21-4-1985. Facts and circumstances of Writ Petition No.2746 of 1997 are therefore distinguishable from those of the Writ Petition No.1481 of 1994. The Writ Petition No.3773 of 1996 and 3834 of 1999 are factually and substantially not same with that of the Writ Petition No.1481 of 1994 and hence principle of res judicata is not applicable in these three Writ Petitions.

145. Mr Anwar Hossain was appointed a Minister on 23-6-1996 and clause (3) of Article 147 came into play to his office on and from 23-6-1996 disqualifying him to hold any other office, post or position of profit or emolument or take any part whatsoever in the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object.

146. While Mr Akhtar Imam and Abdur Razzaque Learned Advocates for the petitioner, have argued that by operation of clause (3) of Article 147. Mr Anwar Hossain was disqualified to hold the offices of Printer and Publisher, Editor and Executive Director-Il as those are offices of profit, Mr Rafique-ul-Huq has argued that the disqualification will be effective in future and not in the existing offices, i.e. if Mr Anwar Hossain wanted to hold any new office of profit simultaneously holding the office of a Minister he was disqualified. But he shall not cease to hold those offices of profit which he held before entering upon the office of a Minister. According to him, those offices are not offices of profit.

147. Mr Akhtar Imam and Mr Abdur Razzaque have argued that the office of a Minister itself is an office of profit, but the proviso to clause (3) of Article 147 has saved that office from the ambit of clause (3) and, as such, the office of a Minister shall not be deemed to be an office of profit. Mr Rafiqul- Huq, on the other hand, has argued that the proviso has saved the existing offices of Mr Anwar Hossain. His assertive submission is that the post of Editor, Printer and Publisher and the Executive Director-Il are neither offices of profit nor Article 147(3) applies in the case of Mr Anwar Hossain.

148. Mr Anwar Hossain wrote a letter to the Deputy Commissioner (should be the District Magistrate), Dhaka on 26-8-1996 as it appears from Annexure-E to the Writ Petition No.2746 of 1997 informing that he had appointed Mr Rahat Khan as the Editor-in-charge of the Daily Ittefaq. On 4-2-1997 the Additional District Magistrate, in response to his letter dated 26-8-1996 wrote a letter to Mr Anwar Hossain (Annexure-E) addressing him as the publisher of the Daily Ittefaq and informing that the office of the District Magistrate had no objection to the appointment of Mr Rahat Khan as Editor-in- charge. Mr Mainul Hosein raised objections to the District Magistrate on several counts that Mi Anwar Hossain had ceased to be the Editor of the Daily lttefaq and that he was publisher on behalf of the Company and that there was no scope in law to recognise someone as Editor-in-charge and that there was no concept in the Act, 1973 like Editor-in- charge, etc. (Annexure-F). The Additional District Magistrate had asserted by his letter dated 3-4-1997 that Mr Anwar Hossain by virtue of Declaration dated 21-4-1985 was the publisher and printer of the Daily Ittefaq and the publisher will alone decide by whom he shall run the newspaper. No Declaration was necessary for change of Editor in Law (Annexure-G). Thereafter, Mr Anwar Hossain had re-instated a suspended accounts officer' on 25-9-1999, suspended a senior security officer on 23-1-1999, appointed Mr Showkat Hossain Masum in the Finance Page of the Daily Ittefaq on 17-8-1999.

149. I have already observed that there is no analogous corresponding provision in the Constitution of Pakistan, India or the United States to Article 147(3). In addition to the commentary made by Mr Mahmudul Islam, referred to above, the learned Advocates for the petitioner have placed their reliance upon some reported cases eventually dealing with Article 147(3).

150. In the case of M Saleem Ullah, Advocate vs Justice Mohammad Abdul Quddus Chowdhury and another referred to above the respondent Mohammad Abdul Quddus Chowdhury was appointed as an Additional Judge of the High Court Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court on 17-1- 1983 and on 1-3-1983 he was appointed as Secretary.Law and Parliamentary Affairs Division which is now the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs. Ground of violation of Article 147(3) was raised, amongst others, in the said Writ Petition and their Lordships found that clause (3) of Article 147 is applicable to the office of a Judge of the Supreme Court and that the office of the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs is an office of profit. But their Lordships held that "Consequently, notwithstanding the fact that the appointment of a Judge of the Supreme Court as Secretary to the Ministry of Law and Justice and his continuance in such post is apparently violative of clause (3) of Article 147 of the Constitution, the appointment and continuance of the respondent No. I in the said post has been protected by the proviso to sub-para (2) of para 10 of the Proclamation of 24th March. 1982 read with para 19 of the Fourth Schedule and Article 150 of the Constitution."

151. The salient features of this case are that the respondent Mohammad Abdul Quddus Chowdhury was appointed as an Additional Judge of the Bangladesh Supreme Court under a Martial Law order dated 17-1-1983 and he was appointed Secretary to the Ministry of Law and Justice by another Martial Law Order dated 1-3-1983 when the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was under suspension under Martial Law. The Writ Petition was filed in the year 1989 and the judgment was delivered on 16-1-1989. In spite of the suspension of the Constitution during the impugned orders were made, the High Court Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court has in this case, examined the point whether the Order of appointment of Mr Justice Abdul Quddus Chowdhury to the office of the Secretary, Ministry of Law. Justice and Parliamentary Affairs made by a Martial Law order was violative to the provisions of Article 147(3) and found that the same was 'apparently violative.

152. The Constitution was partially revived on 7-3-1984 by the Martial Law Order No.1 of 1984 namely, the Constitution (partial Revival) Order 1984. Article 102 in truncated form was revived by .the Constitution (partial revival) 2nd Order, 1985. This did not debar the Supreme Court of Bangladesh from examining constitutionality of an order passed under the Martial Law in the year 1983 nor did it-prevent the petitioner from invoking the Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Therefore, the High Court Division may, at any time, examine propriety, legality, constitutionality of any order passed, any action taken, any act done under the cover of violative of any provisions of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh though the Constitution itself at the relevant time remained suspended under the Extra Constitutional Law.

153. This is why this Court may examine whether a Minister of the Martial Law regime, namely, the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain, was competent to make a Declaration to the District Magistrate on 21-4-1985 declaring him to be the Printer and Publisher of the Daily Ittefaq, on behalf of the Ittefaq Group of Publications while he was  holding an office specified in clause (4) of Article 147 and whether the same was violative to Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

154. The framers of the Constitution, in their wisdom, have employed the verb 'shall' in Clause (3) of Article 147 making the provision mandatory for those to whom Clause (4) applies. The word 'shall' is synonym with the word 'must' and, as such, the same is obligatory upon the holders of offices specified in Clause (4) of Article 147.

155. The offices of Printer and Publisher in the Daily Ittefaq are being run with the purpose of .making profit as apparent from the Articles of Association and Memorandum of the lttefaq Group of Publications Limited and in the ordinary parlance of the words like other business offices, the pertinent questions is therefore, whether on 21-4-1985 as holder of specified office Mr Anwar Hossain was disqualified under Article 147(3) to hold any office of profit, namely, the offices of Printer and Publisher of the Daily Ittefaq and if so, whether the Declaration No. 16/85 dated 21-4-1985 made by Mr Anwar Hossain, a specified office holder with the District Magistrate, Dhaka declaring him to be the Printer and Publisher of the Daily lttefaq on behalf of the lttefaq Group of Publications Ltd is violative of Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and void and without any legal effect.

156. The persons specified in Article 147(4) during their tenure in such offices, if violate or offend by their acts or omissions or conduct any constitutional provisions, even during the period when the Constitution itself remained suspended, such acts or omissions of such persons holding such offices, in whatever names they are called, are not immune from Judicial review of the High Court Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court. By exercising powers conferred by the Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh the High Court Division may at any time examine legality, propriety, validity and constitutionality of any act done, any action taken, any, order passed by or omissions on the part of holders of those specified offices irrespective of their public or private nature, since the office itself is a public office and meant for performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic and under Articles 55 of the Constitution the executive powers are exercised by the Ministers.

157. The person who owns or keeps in his possession any press for the printing of books or papers is a Printer under the Definitions section of the Act and the person who in any manner whatsoever, undertakes, is in control of, or is responsible for the publication of any book or paper, is a Publisher which includes the proprietor of the publishing concern.

158. The definitions given in the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 prima facie show that the posts of 'printer' and 'publisher' are posts of profit.

159. The Declaration dated 21-4-1985 was made by the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain with the District Magistrate, Dhaka while he was holding the specified office of a Minister and was suffering from constitutional disability, under Article 147(3) and (4) is therefore, unconstitutional, void, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The Declaration No.16 of 1985 made by Mr Anwar Hossain with the District Magistrate. Dhaka in respect of 'Printer and Publisher' of the Daily Ittefaq is thus struck down being violative of Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

160. Had the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain written the impugned letter to the District Magistrate. Dhaka informing him about appointment of Mr Rahat Khan as Editor-in-Charge of the Daily Ittefaq some time before 23-6-1996 i-e the date on which he entered upon the office of a Minister for the second time, the same would remain beyond the purview of Article 147(3). But he appointed Mr Rahat Khan as Editor-in-Charge M the Daily lttefaq and wrote the letter of information thereof to the District Magistrate, Dhaka after assuming the office of a Minister when disqualifying Article 147(3) came into play on him. Under section 2(d) of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 "editor" means the person who controls the selection of the matter that is published in a newspaper. 'Controlling' and 'Selecting' matter to be published in a newspaper is a managerial function relating to the management of the newspaper. The fact of appointing an Editor-in-charge in a newspaper and writing letter in that regard to the District Magistrate was, in fact, taking part in the management or conduct of the Company, association or body having' profit or gain as its object within the meaning of Article 147(3). The innuendo of the term 'in charge' was that the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain was the actual editor which he was debarred under the mandatory provision of Article 147(3) and, as such, illegal, void without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

161. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, in his Affidavit-in-oppositions and Supplementary Affidavit-in-opposition has contended that the post of Editor in the Daily Ittefaq did never carry salary or emolument and, as such, the same is not office of profit. The learned Advocates for the petitioner have argued that this post carries monthly remuneration and under the Wage Board Award for the Newspapers Employees this post is a salaried post.

162. In response to the submissions of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the petitioner has placed reliance upon the case of Shahid Nabi Malik vs Chief Election Commissioner, reported in PLD 1997(SC) 32 where their Lordships held that "if an office is a regular office on the strength of the department concerned to which salary/emoluments/ allowances are attached, it is an office of profit. A person cannot change the character/nature of such an office by not drawing salary, etc."

163. The learned Advocates for the petitioner then submits that the office of the Editor of the Daily Ittefaq is run for gain or profit and it carries remuneration and, as such, it is an office of profit. no matter whether the respondent has drawn his remuneration attached to this office from the Company's account or not. It will not change the nature and character of the office. Rather, he has admitted that he borrows from the Company from time to time.

164. I therefore, hold that the office of an Editor of a Newspaper is an office of profit and the post of Editor in the Daily Ittefaq is an office of profit. The respondent Mr Anwar Hossain was disabled to hold the office of the Editor of the Daily Ittefaq on and from 27-3-1985 and again on and from 23-6-1996 either by his person or through any Editor-in- charge.

165. The orders passed by the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain and impugned in Writ Petition No.3834 of 1999, namely, suspension from reinstatement to and appointment for the lttefaq Group of Publications Limited while he was holding the office of a Minister amount to taking part in the management and conduct of the Company which he was debarred from by operation of Article 147(3) and, as such, void, illegal without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

166. The Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited being a profit making Company the post and office of the Executive Director-II is also an office of profit. The respondent has time to time borrowed money from this company. The petitioner has stated that the respondent as Executive Director-II would receive monthly remuneration of Taka 12,500 apart from other drawings and the respondent has stated that he did not draw the remuneration attached to this office under a resolution of the Company for the last three years. He has only borrowed from the Company like the Executive Director I.

167. The ratio-decidendi of the case of Shahid Nabi Malik is applicable in this case.

168. In the case of Khorshed Alam vs Azizur Rahman reported in 1995 BLD 639 the term 'Body Corporate' and the question as to whether Managing Director of the Private Limited Company is a 'Public Servant' and could be prosecuted under the provisions of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958 came up for consideration and their Lordship held that "A private limited Company registered under the Companies Act is a 'Body Corporate' and a Managing Director of such a Company is a 'Public Servant' and he could be tried under the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1958." Therefore, the office of the Executive Director in a Private Limited Company is not only an office of profit but simultaneously an office of a 'Public Servant'.

169. This is more important in the case of a Newspaper. "A Newspaper." defined in Black's Law Dictionary. 7th Edition is "A publication for general circulation usually. in sheet form, appearing at regular intervals usually daily or weekly and containing matters of general public interest such as current events" Matters of general public interest is something that distinguishes a newspaper from those of trading companies. This public interest endows a Newspaper with public responsibility and public trust discharge of which is of public nature In section 2(t) of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act 1973. "Newspaper" means any periodical work containing public news or comments on public news". Public news and comments thereof are matters of public importance.

170. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, Learned Senior Advocate, in his affidavit-in-opposition, has stated that the authenticated Declaration of a Newspaper is a Licence and, according to him, the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited could publish the Daily Ittefaq only because Mr Anwar Hossain holds the Licence. If this proposition is accepted, I am afraid it will definitely undermine the role and diminish the importance of a Newspaper for a Licensee has no right, title or interest in the property save and accept the right to use the same on behalf of the real owner (Abul Hasnat & others vs Ershad Ali Beg 42 DLR 244)." This proposition will throw a Newspaper at the mercy of the Licensor who can cancel a Licence on exigencies This must not be the case of a Newspaper.

171. A District Magistrate under section 20 of the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act 1973 can cancel the authentication of a declaration stating some specific reasons, such as if the Printer and Publisher has ceased to be a citizen of Bangladesh convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude: found to be a lunatic or of unsound mind by any Court: or has ceased to have the financial resources required for regularly publishing the newspaper, interfere with administration of law or maintenance of law and order likely to endanger the security of Bangladesh or likely to prejudice the maintenance of friendly relations of Bangladesh with any foreign state by any matter published in the newspaper or is indecent, obscene or defamatory None of these reasons characterise a declaration to a mere Licence.

172. On 27-3-1985 when respondent Mr Anwar Hossain entered upon the specified office under General Ershad regime he lost this office of the Executive Director in the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited forthwith by operation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. This Article came into play again on him on 23-6-1996 as soon as he assumed the office of a Minister.

173. Article 52 of the Articles of Association of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited provides that an Executive Director can nominate someone to discharge his function for temporary period, such as absence from Dhaka due to illness or any other such reason. Respondent Mr Anwar Hossain had nominated firstly, Mr Mohibul Ahsan Shawoon and later his wife Mrs. Tasmima Hossain to act as an Executive Director respectively as his nominee after becoming disqualified so to do for, that amounts to taking part in the management and conduct of the company and, as such, illegal, void and without any legal effect.

174. Mr Abdur Razzaque, learned Advocate for the petitioner, with a view to present before us the Ministerial position in the British Cabinet, has placed the following passages from the book named. 'Constitutional and Administrative Law' written by Helarre Barnett, 3rd Edition. page 414. Financial Probity-The personal financial probity of Ministers, their Parliamentary Private Secretaries and other Members of Parliament is regarded with seriousness. Under the law and custom of Parliament. Members must declare their financial interests in the register of Member's Interests and make public declarations in debate or committee proceedings of any interests they hold which may effect their impartiality. The holding of directorships. ownership of shares, consultancy positions and receipt of gifts all raise issues concerning integrity and fitness for office. Ministers of the Crown must give up any public appointments or directorships on assuming office. Further, they must divest themselves of any financial interest on assuming office where that interest might give rise to conflict with his or her ministerial responsibilities".

175. In 1701, the British Parliament passed 'the Act of Settlement' providing, amongst others, 'no office-holder should sit in the House of Commons'. This Act was repealed by the Place Act, 1707.

76. According to CF Strong, "As it was, the repealing Act the Place Act of 1707-saved the Constitution from this unrealised peril but left the clause operative in two directions. First part of what remained of the clause was secure that no office-holder shall be in position to hold government contracts so that a Cabinet Minister must resign all active interest in any company concerned in such contracts. Secondly, the clause still applies to the Permanent Civil Service no member of which can sit in the Parliament-CF Strong. Modern Political Constitution, 3rd Edition pages 219-20.

177. The House of Commons Disqualification Act, 1975 lists offices of the holders of which are disqualified for membership of the House of Commons.

178. Article 66 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has provided qualification and dis-qualifications for election to the Parliament and in Clause (dd) the Article has provided that a person shall be disqualified who "holds any office of profit in the service of the Republic other than an office which is declared by law not to disqualify its holders". Clause (2A) to this Article was inserted in the year 1978 and this Clause precludes some offices from the ambit of office of profit providing that "For the purposes of this article a person shall not be deemed to hold an office of profit in the service of the Republic by reason only that he is a President. Prime Minister. Minister of State or Deputy Minister"

179. Scope and field of Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh is far more wider than any known Constitution. The reason is obvious. The intention of the framers of the Constitution is articulate and vivid both in expression and meaning. A Judge of the Supreme Court, for instance, if holds a post of a director of a private Limited Company engaged in business for making profit or indulges himself in business affairs while holding the office of a Judge the result is disastrous. So also the case of the President, Prime Minister, Chief Adviser, Speaker or Deputy Speaker, Minister, Adviser, Minister for State. Deputy Minister, etc. whose offices have been specified in Clause (4) of Article 147. The Constitutional offices, in that case, will soon become business offices of profit at the peril of the nation. The specified office holders in the intention of the framers of the Constitution shall devote to the fullest extent and the utmost of their ability to the performance of functions in connection with offices to which they have taken Oath free from all other interests or considerations.

180. This necessarily raises the question how far this disability of the holders of the offices specified in clause (4) of the Article 147 shall continue. Mr Akhtar Imam and Mr Abdul Razzaque submit that the cessation is not temporary in nature but complete cessation. Once the holders of those offices, they argued, ceased to hold any post or office of profit in a Company or Association they shall remain so irrespective of their cessation of the offices specified in clause (4) of Article 147.

181. Mr Akhtar Imam has relied upon the case of Akbar Hassan vs Government of Pakistan reported in PLD 1976 (SC) 315.

Mr Justice Abdul Kadir Sheikh had been a Judge of the Pakistan Supreme Court. By Gazette Notification dated 22-1-1975 he was appointed as the Chief Justice of the High Court of Sind and Baluchistan on deputation. Amongst others, the Gazette Notification provided during the period Mr Justice Abdul Kadir Sheikh holds the office of Chief Justice of the High Court of Sind and Baluchistan he will continue to retain his lien on the office of and seniority as Judge of the Supreme Court. "In a Writ of quo warranto this matter came up for examination and their Lordships held that "Holding of one permanent post precludes the incumbent from holding another post in similar capacity. Respondent Judge admitted by Federal Government to have been appointed as permanent Chief Justice and not as acting Chief Justice. Words on deputation in the Notification and the Paragraph of notification stating that such Judge will continue to retain his lien on the office and seniority as Judge of the Supreme Court is mere surplusage".

Their Lordships further held that "None can hold two substantive offices at same time. Supreme Court Judge appointed as Chief Justice of the High Court deemed to have vacated office of the Judge of the Supreme Court".

It was also held that "No occasion or question of retention of lien or seniority in Supreme Court, Judge if ever to revert to Supreme Court such would be fresh appointment and not continuation of previous appointment",

In this case the Supreme Court of Pakistan refused the lien as surplusage and held that if the incumbent had to revert to his original post it would be a fresh appointment and not continuation. But their Lordships in this case have further held that "a Judge can take temporary assignment outside his normal duties. Judge holding other posts such as Election Commissioner is legal" In fact. Articles 207 and 213 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973 are specific in this respect.

182. The post of a Minister, being carrying emolument, is, no doubt, a substantive post vis-a-vis the post of the Ittefaq Group of Publications Ltd and the Daily Ittefaq.

183. Though the disability and disqualification of the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain evaporated the moment he ceased to be a Minister yet by analogical deduction of the case of Abrar Hassan (supra), he needed to be appointed afresh in his substantive posts and offices in the Daily Ittefaq and in the Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited.

184. Though in the case of Akbar Hassan (supra) lien provided for a Judge was found not available but, in my opinion, it may be available in business offices on the basis of Beneficial Construction theory of Constitution and statute.

185. There is a maxim in Latin that says, "Fiat Justicia, ruat Coelum-Let Justice be done though the Heavens should fall"

After tracing the historical background of the Maxim. Mr Justice Nassim Hussain Shah of the Pakistan Supreme Court, held in the case of Federation of Pakistan vs Md Saifullah Khan reported in PLD 1989 (SC) 166 that "we would prefer to take the first part of the maxim" Fiat Justicia (Let, justice be done) and discard the rest, namely, "ruat coelum" (though the Heavens should fall) because Justice should be done in such a manner that the Heavens should not fall".

186. The Bangladesh Supreme Court, has long ago held that "Justice shall not only be done but it must manifestly and undoubtedly appear that justice has been done."

187. A holder of Office of Profit may keep lien by way of resolution/decision in their respective concern before entering upon the specified offices of Article 147 so that it may automatically revive as soon as he/she ceases to hold specified office.

188. In the case of Shahid Nabi Malik (PLD 1997 (SC) 32) their Lordships have further held that:

"Constitution unlike a statute cannot be changed or amended frequently. A document of such a basic nature is not merely imprisonment of the past but is also alive to the future aspiration and need of the nation."

189. Both Mr Akhtar Imam and Mr Abdur Razzaque have lastly argued that the Additional District Magistrate, Md Safiul Alam, has acted malafide in exercising his Jurisdiction in writing Annexures-E and G to the Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997. Mr Nikilesh Dutta, the Learned Deputy Attorney-General has submitted that Mr Md Safiul Alam while exercising his Jurisdiction under the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 has acted in 'excess of Jurisdiction' so far it relates to the 'Ittefaq Group of Publications Limited in the Declaration itself (Annexure D) and interpretation thereof together with the Act.

190. Referring the. case of Ram Chandra Chowdhury vs Government of West Bengal reported in AIR 1964 (Calcutta) 265. Mr Razzaque submits that malafide does not necessarily involve a malicious intention. It is enough if the aggrieved party establishes (1) that the authority making the impugned order did not apply its mind at all to the matter in question or (2) that the impugned order was made for a purpose or upon a ground other than what is mentioned on the face of the Order.

191. In Writ Petition No. 1481 of 1994 the. Lordships deplored the role of the District Magistrate and admonished him for failure to perform his statutory obligations and failure to see that the 'Daily Ittefaq' is not published with the disqualified person.'

192. Here I find that Mr Safiul Alam, the Learned Additional District Magistrate. Dhaka has utterly failed to understand and interpret the Declaration No. 16 of 1985 and in writing the impugned Annexure-G has acted more like an Administrator rather than a Magistrate. 1st Class though the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 has entrusted the responsibility upon a Magistrate. 1 st Class (District Magistrate) and not upon an Administrator or Collector of Revenue. Failure of the Additional Deputy Commissioner or Additional Deputy Collector or for that matter, administrator to perform the Magisterial Judicial functions though deplorable but not unanticipated for, most of them are not even Law graduates nor acquainted from their studentship with the law, legal history, legal norms, legal tradition and legal system. The Learned Additional District Magistrate. Dhaka while applied for a job in his career applied for the Administrative Cadre and appointed and raised as such and exercising the Magisterial Judicial power or Jurisdiction, appears in this case is nothing but fallacy of English Legal system of administration of Criminal Justice introduced by Warren Hastings in the colonial days and strengthened by Cornwallis, a defeated and wounded British General in the American War of Independence at the hands of George Washington, This colonial legacy is still prevailing even after more 32 years of our National Independence in the name of administration of Criminal Justice, Illegality committed by the Learned Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka is due to his inability to perform the Judicial functions which vices are .inherent in nature and that remind us how earnestly and urgently separation of judiciary is needed.

193. As I have observed with reference to the case of S & C Company vs Union of India, (Supra), that freedom of Press means freedom of readers to read impartial news and reports in a newspaper, I hold that the respondent Mr Anwar Hossain has violated the freedom of press guaranteed by Article 39 of the Constitution by interfering in the management of the Daily Ittefaq firstly, by claiming himself to be the Printer and Publisher, secondly, by claiming himself to be the Editor while he was disqualified to be so and thirdly, by appointing an Editor-in-charge and by causing its stoppage from 28-12-1993 to 13-1-1994 and also by exerting his Ministerial authority, power and position in the management and administration of the Daily Ittefaq from 1985-90 and 1996-01. The authoritative powers were thus abused.

194. In the result, Rules issued in these three Writ Petitions are made absolute without any order as to costs.

Since we have differed with each other, let the record of the case be placed before the learned Chief Justice for necessary order.

Mr Akhtar Imam and Mr Abdur Razzaque, learned Counsels for the petitioner, have raised important question of interpretation of statute i.e. sections 2( d), 6, 7 and 12 of the Printing Press and Publication (Declaration. and Registration) Act, 1973 and interpretation of Articles 39 and 147(3).
