Rather, section 6 of the Act of 1973 has made it imperative that the Editor's name must be printed in every copy of the newspaper, that without having his name printed as Editor none can remain or continue to be an Editor, that the name of Mr Anwar Hossain is not being printed as Editor and, as such, he is no longer the Editor of the daily Ittefaq and that the name of Mr Rahat Khan is being printed in the Printers Line and he is the editor and in this behalf he (Mr Mainul Hosein) has given a declaration. This Annexure-F dated 12-3-97 has evoked/prompted the writing of Annexure-G dated 1-4-97 by the Additional District Magistrate Dhaka to Mr Mainul Hosein and it is argued by the learned Counsel for the petitioner that Annexure-G not being a refusal to authenticate a declaration made under section 12 of the Act of 1973 the contention of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, learned Counsel for respondent Mr Anwar Hossain that instead of a writ petition an appeal against the refusal to authenticate ought to have been preferred is misconceived. I find force and substance in the arguments of Mr Imam and Mr Razzaque and it is accepted.

<u>225. For the sake of convenience, before going into the other arguments of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, I propose to discuss the 4 (four) following arguments advanced by him even at the risk of some repetition. The first argument is, that the Rules in Writ Petition Nos. 3773 of 1996 and 3834 of 1999 are not maintainable under Article 102(2)(a) of the Constitution. Because the impugned acts by Mr Anwar Hossain were not done in the exercise of his powers and functions in the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority rather, if at all, those were done in relation to the affairs of the daily Ittefaq which is a private limited company. In support of this argument, Mr Huq referred to the case of Sultana Nahar, Advocate vs Bangladesh and others reported in 1998 BLD 363. It was a case involving the eviction of 600 sex workers from a brothel called "Kandu Patti" by an unruly mob led by the local ward commissioner, one Mr Hossain, under the very nose of the law enforcing agencies and the Senior Judge made the Rule absolute declaring that the sex workers were illegally and forcibly evicted and the law enforcing agencies failed to discharge their legal duties by not giving legal protection to them (sex workers) to continue their profession at "Kandu Patti" with a direction to respondent Nos. 1, 2, 8 and 9 to earmark a specified and distinct area for their permanent rehabilitation. There was also a mandatory injunction as a stopgap arrangement to restore possession of the evicted sex workers till their rehabilitation, with a further direction to respondent No.5, officer-in-charge, Kotwali Police Station, Dhaka to lodge an FIR, according to the written complaint of 14 sex workers. This was dissented to by the learned Junior Judge holding, inter alia, that the manner of eviction of the sex workers though is condemnable, this Court, in its writ jurisdiction, is unable to restore their possession because, the place is owned by a private individual and that the Government has now lost its jurisdiction to rehabilitate the sex workers since the action done was not in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority attracting the mischief of Article 102(1 )(9). This decision, I am afraid, cannot be made applicable in the instant case simply because the eviction was carried out by some unruly mob led by the local Ward Commissioner who was neither a person exercising any function in the Affairs of the Republic nor did do anything in discharge of his public duty.</u>

<u>226. Mr Anwar Hossain, the respondent, while holding the post of a Minister, as I have referred to above, has not only taken part in the management of the daily Ittefaq, he has also caused interference in the publication of the paper for long 16(sixteen) days with a view to forcing and compelling the Editor-in-charge and others to print his name as Publisher/Editor. Both Mr Akhtar Imam and Abdur Razzaque argued that a Minister may not be a person in the service of the Republic but, surely and definitely, he has constitutional functions and thus exercises very high public duty. By causing the closure and or stoppage of printing of the paper</u>

<u>from 28-12-1993 to 13-1-1994 he (Mr Anwar Hossain) had violated Article 39 of the Constitution and that brought his action fairly and squarely within the ambit of both Article 102(1) and 102(2) and the writ petition cannot be said to be not maintainable. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq argued that Mr Anwar Hossain did, if at all, do something in connection with the affairs of the Ittefaq and not in connection with the Affairs of the Republic or any local body or authority. True it is that the actions of Mr Anwar Hossain primarily affected the affairs of the company, but at the same time it did affect the readers of the paper who have a right to read fair, neutral objective and impartial news and views which is guaranteed under Article 39(2)(b) of the Constitution. It is inescapable to avoid the mischief of Article 39 which is one of the Articles under Chapter III i.e. fundamental rights and hence, there is an infringement of fundamental right under Article 102 which can be invoked by operation or Article 44 of the Constitution. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq also argued that the post of Executive Editor is not a post of profit and, as such, there can be no bar in holding this post while Mr Anwar Hossain became a Minister. I have already dealt with this point that from a plain reading of the 5th Wage Board Award, 1997 it is evident that the said post is a post of profit. Mr Akhtar Imam has taken me through the Articles and Memorandum of Association of the company and with reference to Article 50 argued that the directors may from time to time appoint anyone of their body as the Managing Director provided that the Director shall not take any appointment made or committee constituted under Articles 51 and 52. Article 51 deals with managing agent stating that the directors may at any time appoint agent to manage the entire affairs of the company under the control and direction of the directors upon such terms as they think fit subject to the provisions of this Act provided the director shall not make any appointment under this Article during the subsistence of any appointment made or committee constituted under Article 50 and/or 52. Article 52 deals with Executive Committee and Executive Directors, Providing that company in general meeting may appoint from amongst directors one or more directors to be Executive Director or Directors and may constitute an Executive Committee consisting of such executive director/directors as it thinks fit. Provided that no appointment of an Executive Director shall be made or constitution of an Executive Committee shall be made during the subsistence of any appointment earlier made under Article 50 and/or 51. While clause (d) provides that for the purpose of division of responsibility between Executive Directors, the company's business shall be taken to comprise of the following sections:</u>

<u>(i) Press and Publications.</u>

<u>(ii) Accounts,</u>

<u>(iii) General Section comprising of:</u>

<u>(a) Circulation Department.</u>

<u>(b) Advertisement Department.</u>

<u>(c) Job Department and Purchase Department.</u>

<u>Clause (E) provides that the respective responsibilities of the Executive Director in respect of each. of the sections referred to above shall be defined by the Company in General Meeting and Clause (F) provides that in the event of an Executive Director being unable to discharge his functions due to absence from Dhaka or illness or any other such reason he may nominate, in writing, another Director to exercise his functions during such absence. The expression "due to absence from Dhaka or illness or any other such reason" cannot and must not be allowed to mean during his absence so long he remains a member of the Cabinet.</u>

<u>227. Mr Akhtar Imam argued that a combination of the Executive Directors I and II constituted the post of Managing Director and the argument advanced by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq that there is no post of Managing Director in the Ittefaq Group of Publication is not tenable in law in view of the discussions made above. The second point raised by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq is that since there are three Civil Suits pending between the same parties on the same point as in the writ petitions, all the three Rules are liable to be discharged as those are not maintainable, inasmuch as the petitioner cannot be allowed to invoke both writ jurisdiction and remedies available in the civil Court. Mr Huq has furnished me with a copy showing the details of cases filed by Mr Mainul Hosein. From the said list it appears that serial Nos. 5,6 and 14 are three civil suits i.e. (a) Title Suit No. 59 of 2002, (b) Title Suit No. 84 of 2002 and (c) Title Suit No. 321 of 2002 and the date of filing of the aforesaid three suits are as follows: 11-3-2002, 7-4-2002 and 24-11-2002. So, all the three suits were instituted subsequent to the filing of the three writ petitions. To counter this argument advanced by Mr Huq, Mr Akhtar Imam learned Counsel for the petitioner, has placed reliance on the case of Chairman Civil Aviation Authority vs Kazi Abdur Rouf reported in 46 DLR (AD) 145. The reported case is different and distinguishable from the writ petition before us inasmuch as, in the reported case one Kazi A. Rouf, Headmaster and Secretary of the Staff Welfare High School filed a writ petition challenging a Memo dated 29-7-92 of the School Inspector, Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Dhaka to the Chairman, Bangladesh Civil Aviation Authority, Kurmitola requesting the latter to form an Ad hoc Committee in terms of regulation 20 of the Board contending that the Managing Committee could have been constituted in terms of Regulation 4(1) and not in terms of Regulation 20(1). The writ petitioner challenged the impugned memo in a Title Suit and having lost in the injunction matter lost faith in the civil Court and then filed a writ petition and Mr Justice Mustafa Kamal, as his Lordship then was, held that there is no bar in filing writ petition after withdrawing a suit. It all depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. But it is clear that in the present case writ petitioner filed a suit basically containing highly contentious and disputed question of facts for adjudication by a civil Court and it is not his case before the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction that his grievance can be met merely by looking at law on agreed facts, so the pursuit of suit is unnecessary. He came to lay before the writ jurisdiction the same question offact which he earlier laid before the civil Court for adjudication. The writ jurisdiction shall have been denied to him under such circumstances. Mr Imam argued that this decision by implication has held that if there is no disputed question of fact the door of writ jurisdiction is not closed . And in the Civil Suits and the three writ petitions there is no disputed question of facts. The suits and the writ petitions rather involved interpretation of a statute i.e. the Printing Press and Publication (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 and the interpretations of Article 39 and Article 147(3) and its proviso. Furthermore, in the instant case, as I have already referred to earlier, the suits having been filed subsequent to the filing of the writ petitions, the arguments advanced by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq that since suits are pending so writ petitions cannot be maintained because under Article 110 of the Constitution all the suits ought to have been brought before this Court for disposal simultaneously. This argument, I am constrained to hold, cuts both ways. It imposes no unilateral or singular obligation on the writ petitioner to file an application under Article 110, inasmuch as, a co-equal and corresponding right has been made available by the aforesaid Article to the respondent as well and the respondent could have, if so advised, brought those suits for adjudication by one and the same Court i.e. the High Court Division. Neither party having done so, this contention of Mr Huq does not appeal to me. In reply to the second point raised by Mr Haq mainly that during the pendency of the civil suits these writ petitions are not maintainable, Mr Akhtar Imam has referred to the case of Dhaka Warehouse Limited and another vs Assistant Collector of Customs and another reported in 1991 BLD (AD) 327 wherein their Lordships held that in principle, where an alternative statutory remedy is available, application under Article 102 may not be entertained to circumvent a statutory procedure. There are however, exceptions to this rule. Without attempting an exhaustive enumeration of complete extraordinary situation we may note a view of them. In spite of an alternative statutory remedy, an aggrieved person may take recourse to Article 102 of the Constitution where the vires of a statute or a statutory provision is challenged, where alternative remedy is not efficacious or adequate and the wrong complained of is so inextricably mixed up that the High Court Division may for the prevention of public injury and the vindication of public justice examine that complaint. It is needless to add that the High Court Division is to see that the aggrieved person must have good reason for bypassing an alternative remedy. Mr Imam also placed reliance on the case of MA Hai, Md Wazed Ali Mia and Md Moslem vs Trading Corporation of Bangladesh. In that case also it was held that availability of alternative remedy by way of appeal or revision will not stand in the way of invoking writ jurisdiction raising purely a question of law or interpretation of statutes. In the reported case the appellant Abdul Hai, a Senior Executive of the TCB, was provisionally removed from service for inefficiency and corruption. A writ petition was filed under Article 102 against the order of removal taking the ground that under the mandatory provision of Rule 7(11) of the Government Servant (Disciplinary and Appeal) Rules, 1984 he stood discharged from the charge because the specified period is 120 days from the date of communication of the charge-sheet to him within which period the proceeding against him was to be concluded, expired before the impugned order of removal was passed. He claimed that the Disciplinary and Appeal Rules of 1984 are applicable to him since the corporation adopted the rules. The corporation stressed that the proceedings were presented under the Rules of 1976, which did not provide for any time limit, such as 120 days from the date of submission of charge-sheet or 120 days from the date of suspension of the accused. Some other grounds were also taken. The High Court Division upheld the contention of the corporation that the provisions of Rule VII, sub-rule 2 of the Rules of 1984 are applicable and all the writ petitions were dismissed. As against that, the petitioners preferred the instant appeal and their Lordships held that if the writ jurisdiction is sought to be invoked raising purely a question of law or interpretation of stature, as in these cases, availability of an alternative remedy will not stand in the way. In the case before me admittedly the facts are not in dispute and the civil suits as well as the writ petitions call for interpretation of various sections of the statute namely, the Printing Press and Publication (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 as well as . the interpretation of some Articles of the Constitution including Articles 39 and 147(3) hence the alternative remedy, as argued by Mr Huq, shall not stand in the way of the writ petitions.</u>

228. The third point argued by Mr Huq is that the Rule in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 is liable to be discharged for the petitioner's failure to invoke and to exhaust the alternative statutory remedy by way of appeal before the Press Appellate Board as provided under section 12A of the Printing Press and Publication (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973. This point having been elaborately dealt with before, needs no more discussion except saying that Annexure "G" not being a refusal to authenticate the declaration under section 12(3) the same is not an appealable order.

229. The fourth argument of Mr Huq is that Rule in Writ Petition No. 2746 of 1997 is hit by the principle of res judicata inasmuch as, the point involved in the present Rule has already been decided against the petitioner by judgment and order dated 6-2-2001 passed in Writ Petition No. 1481 of 1994 and the petitioner did not prefer any appeal against the said judgment.

230. Mr Akhtar Imam and Abdur Razzaque have refuted this contention of Mr Rafique-ul-Huq. Firstly, by saying that the point involved in the two writ petitions are neither the same nor have the Judges of the Division Bench in disposing of Writ Petition No. 1481 of 1994 decided the question of disability or disqualification of a Minister to hold any post of profit or emolument after his assumption of the office of a minister rather, their Lordships left that Constitutional question unanswered. On a reference to the said judgment dated 6-2-2001 at pages 16 and 17 of the certified copy of the judgment it is found that their Lordships have observed as follows:

"However, in view of provisions of Article 147(3) which runs as under-No person appointed to or acting in any office to which this Article applies shall hold any office, post or position of profit or emolument or take any part whatsoever for the management or conduct of any company, association or body having profit or gain as its object. It appears that any person holding or acting in any office to which this Article applies shall not hold any office or take any part in the management or conduct of any company. In the instant case, it appears that during the period respondent No.3 (meaning thereby Mr Anwar Hossain) was holding office of the Minister, also continued to print his name as 'printer' and 'publisher' of the daily Ittefaq which leads (sic) to show, participation in the management and conduct in the business and the affairs of the company having profit and gain. The Respondent No.1 (District Magistrate) having been invited earlier by the petitioner, through his letter dated 21-1-92 evidenced by Annexure-F ought to have taken notice of the fact that respondent No.3 was holding the office of printer and publisher as well as the office of the Minister simultaneously and hence ought to have enquired into the matter and examine (sic) as to whether there was any violation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution at all and thus respondent No.1 (the District Magistrate, Dhaka) failed to see that the daily Ittefaq is not published by the disqualified person."

This being the finding, 1 do not find any reason to hold that the constitutional point raised in the writ petition i.e. the disqualification under Article 147(3) has been decided in Writ Petition No.1481. As such, the question of res judicata does not arise Mr Rafique-ul-Huq has also argued that the petitioner instead of filing writ petition seeking a Writ of quo warranto and questioning as to under what authority Mr Anwar Hossain was holding the post of minister, challenged the retention of his post which he held prior to becoming a minister Mr Huq though admits that Article 147(3) puts a complete and total embargo upon the holding of any post of profit or emolument by the constitutional functionaries enumerated in sub-Article (4) of Article 147 of the Constitution, the bar has been removed and or taken away by the proviso to the said Article i.e. 147(3), and, according to Mr Huq, there is no bar for a Minister or other functionaries mentioned above to retain any post or position which he held prior to becoming a Minister as it happened in case of Mr Anwar Hossain and hence he is not required to give up the post held earlier because the proviso imposed a bar in accepting any post of profit after someone becomes a Minister. Besides that, Mr Huq has argued that there is a marked distinction and difference between Article 104 of the Constitution of Pakistan of 1962 and Article 147(3) of the Bangladesh Constitution. In the Pakistan Constitution there is also an embargo in the retention of post of profit by Constitutional functionaries such as the President, Minister and Governor employing expression as the Minister, Governor, etc. shall cease to hold any office of profit whereas under Article 147(3) of the Constitution of Bangladesh the expression is couched in a different language providing that no person appointed to or acting in any office to which this Article applies shall hold any office, post, position of profit or emolument or take any part whatsoever in the management or conduct of any company association or body having profit or gain as its object.Mr Huq argued that the intention of the lawmakers as it appears from the expression used in Article 147, was not to prohibit a Minister from retaining any post or position he held before becoming Minister rather, the intention was to make it applicable to any post of profit after someone becomes a Minister and, in support of his contention, has referred to the case of Md Abdul Haque vs Fazlul Kader Chowdhury reported in 15 DLR 353 and 16 DLR (SC) 52 which I have discussed at an earlier stage.

231. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq also argued that after Mr Anwar Hossain having ceased to be a minister the determination of the constitutional question under Article 147(3) became purely hypothetical and an academic one and, in support of his argument placed reliance on the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR 319. It is not disputed that in the reported case a hypothetical question was decided by the High Court Division and that was why in paragraphs 58 and 59 of the judgment Mr Justice ATM Afzal, as his Lordship then was, eviscerated the said Judgment in the pronouncement as under:

Naimuddin J: In his judgment found that the Upazila Parishad was not a local Government institution within the meaning of Articles 59 and 9 of the Constitution and, as such, Article 9 cannot be invoked for declaring the repealing Ordinance/Act void under Article 7(2) on the ground of inconsistency with . Article 9. He has not also found that the impugned Ordinance/Act is in conflict with any other provision of Part II of the Constitution containing Fundamental Principles of State Policy. That being so, it was wholly unnecessary to decide whether in view of the provision in sub-article (2) of Article 8 that the principles set out in Part II shall not be judicially enforceable, any legislative act which is in direct conflict with and passed in flagrant violation of the provisions of Part II can be declared void under Article 7(2). Having answered this hypothetical question in the affirmative after taking hypothetical facts into consideration in a lengthy discussion, the learned Judge addressed himself to the real question thus;

"Consequently, if it is found that the impugned repealing Ordinance is violative of Article 9 of the Constitution, it is liable to be struck down as void in view of Article 7(2) of the Constitution."

232. Then the finding was made that the repealing Ordinance was not violative of Article 9 with which we have agreed. Therefore, the broad decision that a law can be declared void in case of a conflict with any provision of Part II of the Constitution was uncalled for and made on hypothetical facts. This, as a rule, the Courts always abhor. The Court does not answer merely academic questions but confines itself only to the point/points which are strictly necessary to be decided for the disposal of the matter before it. This should be more so when Constitutional questions are involved and the Court should be ever discreet in such matters. Unlike a civil suit, the practice in Constitutional cases has always been that if the matter can be decided by deciding one issue only no other point need be decided.

Finally, I wish to express my full agreement with the main judgment prepared by the learned Chief Justice."

233. But the issue we are dealing with is neither hypothetical nor academic. I, for one, do not have the slightest hesitation to hold that this is a down-to-earth practical issue and recurrence of such incident may be there again as it did happen twice in the case of Mr Anwar Hossain.

In his Law on Writs, VG Ram Chandran (Fifth Edition) under the caption "Futile writs" at page 984 the author with reference to the case of Munindra Kumar vs Rajiv Govil reported in (1991) 3 SCC 386 (374): AIR 1991 (SC) 1607 said that the selection process adopted by the State Electricity Board having been found to be arbitrary and ultra vires the rule, in view of the fact that even if three more posts (for three petitioners) would have been ordered to be created to afford chance to all the candidates similarly situated, there was a remote chance of the writ petitioners being selected. The Supreme Court therefore, did not issue a Rule observing that "such exercise would be in futility".

The author then said. "This however, does not mean that in no case the Court can consider a question of discretion and not of jurisdiction of the Court (reference may be made to Madhu Limaye's case).

<u>234. In an appropriate case, the Court may also pronounce the constitutionality of a statute even though it may not be necessary in that case. Thus, if a petition is filed by the petitioner against an order passed by the Government withdrawing the benefit granted in favour of the petitioner and that order is revoked, the petition may become infructuous. But if again, that benefit is withdrawn, the petition will not become infructuous. Similarly, although the order has already been passed but if it has a continuing adverse effect on the right of the petitioner, the petition does not become academic in nature. Again, the principle may not apply to an order which is wholly illegal or without jurisdiction.</u>

235. The 2(two) most ticklish points for consideration in these Writ Petitions are the interpretation of Article 147(3), its proviso and the feasibility of the issuance of a Rule under Article 102 of the Constitution against a private person and also interpretation of certain sections including those of sections 2(d), 6, 7 and 12 of the Printing Press and Publication (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973. The proviso in question is in the following language : "provided that such person shall not for the purposes of this clause be deemed to hold any such office, post or position by reason only that he holds or is acting in the office above mentioned. According to Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the embargo or prohibition imposed under Article 147(3) has been lifted or removed by the proviso and, as such, for Mr Anwar Hossain, as a Minister, there was no bar to retain the post and position he held before becoming a minister and that the disqualification only applies to his holding any future post or position of profit after assuming of the office of a minister which is seriously contested by the learned Counsels for the petitioner. According to them, this embargo is a total and complete bar and they have referred to the Constitutional Law of Bangladesh Second Edition by Mr Mahmudul lslam at para 659B under the heading special provisions relating to some constitutional offices of the President, Prime Minister, Speaker, etc (discussed beforehand).

236. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq further submits that Mr Mainul Hosein as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 84 of 2002 in the Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka against Mr Anwar Hossain and others seeking a declaration that in the absence of a fresh resolution by the Board of Directors Mr Anwar Hossain cannot be said to be holding the post of Executive Director-II of the company and the Editor of the Daily Ittefaq. Defendant Mr Anwar Hossain filed an application for stay of further proceedings under section 10 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that analogous and co-related matters are involved in Writ Petition No. 3773 of 1996, 2746 of 1997 and 3834 of 1999 and those are pending in the High Court Division and the learned Joint District Judge allowed the prayer for stay of the suit. As against that, Mr Mainul Hosein preferred Civil Revision No. 5119 of 2002 and their Lordships held "Although we are not in a position to hold that the matters substantially and directly in issue in the present suit and the matters directly and substantially in issue in the Writ petitions are the same, we are constrained to hold that matters involved in these Writ petitions touching the legality or otherwise of some actions of opposite party No.1 and his position as Executive Director-II of the Company are sub-judice before the High Court Division, the position that boiled down in that analogous and co-related matters in such circumstances (sic) the learned Subordinate Court may feel handicapped and totally fettered (sic) to proceed with the present suit pending decisions in the three writ petitions between the contending parties and accordingly, stayed further proceedings of Title Suit No. 84 of 2002 till disposal of the writ petitions and discharged the Rule. Mention may be made here that Title Suit No. 84 of 2002 was filed long after the filing of the writ petitions and because of the order of stay of all further proceedings of the suit there cannot be any risk of conflicting decisions. Mention may also be made that in the Civil Revision their Lordships also held that moreover the judgment delivered by this Court in Writ Petition NO.1481 of 1994 has practically spelt out the position of opposite party No.1 (Mr Anwar Hossain) as the Executive Director-Il of the Company with reference related to (sic) the provisions of Article 147(3) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. We are not, therefore, called upon to elaborate it". It may not be out of place to mention that in Writ Petition NO.1481 of 1994 their Lordships held "the respondent No.1 (District Magistrate. Dhaka) having been notified earlier by the petitioner (Mr Mainul Hosein) through his letter dated 21-1-92 evidenced by Annexure-F ought to have taken notice of the fact that respondent No.3 (Mr Anwar Hossain) was holding the office of Printer and Publisher as well as the office of the Minister simultaneously and hence, ought to have enquired into the matter and examined as to whether there was any violation of Article 147(3) of the Constitution at all and thus respondent No.1 (Additional District Magistrate. Dhaka) failed  to see that the Daily Ittefaq is not published with the disqualified person." It is thus, obvious that the impugned orders and the Rules in the 2 (two) writ petitions are not the same and, as such, the issue remained unresolved.

237. Regard being had to the facts and circumstances, the materials on record, the submissions of the learned Counsels for the parties arid for the foregoing reasons. I agree with my learned brother Mr Abdus Salam Mamun J.

238. In the result, the Rules are made absolute without any order as to cost. All the impugned orders are therefore, declared to have been made or passed without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

Since the matter in dispute involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, a certificate is hereby issued under' Article 103(2)(a) to enable the respondent to prefer an appeal from the judgment and order passed by me and, in the meantime, the parties are directed to maintain status quo in all respects.
